articles.title_orig: U.N. Live Updates: Iran’s President to Make Speech to General Assembly After Trump’s Threat
articles.title_zh: U.N. Live Updates: Iran’s President to Make Speech to General Assembly After Trump’s Threat
articles.content_orig:
In his speech to the United Nations General Assembly on Tuesday, President Donald Trump spun a familiar web of rhetoric regarding U.S. foreign policy—one that highlights force as a method of achieving peace.
In a speech that moved from Iran to Venezuela, Cuba, and beyond, Trump presented something approaching a foreign-policy doctrine: American military might is not the alternative to diplomacy but the leverage that makes it possible.
David Satterfield, Director of Rice University's Baker Institute for Public Policy, tells TIME that the speech Tuesday demonstrates a position held by the Trump Administration that “force is the only currency of value.”
“The strong do as they will and the weak suffer as they must,” he says, further characterizing the approach.
In Trump’s telling, strength is not merely a deterrent. It is something to be used—through military action and economic isolation—to force negotiations or impose an outcome.
How Trump defines ‘peace through strength’
Trump has repeatedly distilled his foreign policy strategy into three words: “peace through strength.” The examples he gave of this policy in action illustrate how he may see the U.S. functioning as a global enforcer going forward.
His definition of the phrase has previously been suggested by its use in Department of Defense ads and in his online endorsements of fellow Republicans. He recently credited this approach for the joint U.S.-Israel strikes that initiated the current conflict with Iran, posting to Truth Social in March: “PEACE THROUGH STRENGTH TO PUT IT MILDLY!!!”
Trump’s approach also encompasses economic coercion. In the case of Iran, he said the U.S. had initially offered economic cooperation, turned to military action when Tehran refused, and was now seeking its “complete economic isolation” to push it back toward negotiations.
Trump grouped Cuba among those affected by U.S. economic pressure campaigns on Tuesday. He described a government under mounting strain and predicted political change, declaring that Cuba was a “failed” nation but that “freedom will be coming.” Cuban delegates departed in protest.
Yet Trump presented such coercion as compatible with his role as a global peacemaker. He claimed credit for resolving eight wars since returning to office, although that claim has been widely disputed.
In tandem, these elements suggest that Trump sees taking action as a superior means of enacting change. He proposes the approaches as being almost diametrically opposed: While others only speak of making a difference, he acts.
“While others have spoken of peace, I have made peace. While others have ignored threats, I have confronted them,” Trump said in front of the General Assembly. “While others have talked of courage, America has shown it.”
Satterfield says that this speech is mostly “old wine rebottled” for Trump. But it clarified how the President is applying his longstanding ideas today: using military action and economic coercion not merely to deter adversaries, but to force negotiations and shape political outcomes.
Trump defends military force against Iran and drug cartels
While Trump sees Iran as an example of his “peace through strength” ethos, the conflict is ongoing, and it remains to be seen how it fits into the pattern that he is hoping to establish.
Addressing the topic seemed all but unavoidable heading into the General Assembly. In doing so, Trump said that he had a choice ahead of him: Move forward with a peace deal or “annihilate the Islamic Republic.”
The comments came amid stalled negotiations in the war that the U.S. and Israel launched in February.
“Will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild and create a far greater country than it ever was before, maybe one of the greatest in the Middle East or even the world?” he asked. “Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic, and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again?”
Members of Iran’s delegation walked out during Trump’s remarks, an immediate demonstration of the gulf between his coercive message and the adversary that he may hope to persuade by it.
In his speech, he also issued threats against cartel leaders, defending his campaign of drone strikes against suspected drug boats in the Caribbean. These strikes have been criticized by international organizations, legal experts, and human rights groups, which state that the military actions violate international law and constitute extrajudicial killings.
“The cartels are the ISIS of the Western Hemisphere—not good people,” he said. “Like ISIS, they should be killed, exiled, or detained as enemy combatants without the possibility of release, which is what we’re doing.”
But while these messages are largely meant to promote the very strength that Trump relies upon in his endeavors, the potency of his remarks may be dwindling amid contested claims of success.
Venezuela is Trump’s ‘peace through strength’ model. But Iran is testing its limits
Kristian Coates Ulrichsen, a fellow for the Middle East at the Baker Institute, tells TIME that Trump’s speech seems “consistent with the narrative of American dominance” that he has long used to justify military action.
Trump suggested Tuesday that he considers Venezuela a leading example. In January, the U.S. military launched Operation Absolute Resolve—a nighttime raid in Caracas that captured Venezuela’s president Nicolás Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores. Both were transported to New York City to face federal drug-trafficking indictments.
The move paved the way for a transition of power in Venezuela, with former Vice President Delcy Rodríguez ascending to the role of acting President. It also led to an August agreement giving a U.S.-linked venture a controlling stake and long-term development rights in fields containing an estimated 65 billion barrels of oil. Trump said the deal “more than doubles” American oil reserves.
“We’re working closely with the leaders of Venezuela to forge a much better future for the Venezuelan people,” Trump said in his speech. “Last month we signed the largest oil deal in history, covering 65 billion barrels of oil, which will benefit both Venezuela and the United States enormously.”
Trump also suggested that U.S. actions had established peace and a route to prosperity for Venezuelans. However, with an acting President who is yet to be elected making deals that may take years to reach fruition, and are likely to draw legal challenges in the meantime, the full picture remains to be seen.
But there is one thing the Venezuela operation might have helped accomplish, which is to establish a potential pattern of a U.S. foreign policy that is defined by unilateral intervention. Following a large show of force, Trump has been quick to claim victory, even while the impact of U.S. involvement is still playing out for the people whom it directly affects.
Another example is the conflict between Israel and Hamas. In his remarks, Trump gave himself credit for ending the war in Gaza, even though key aspects of the peace deal Trump helped broker in October 2025—including Hamas’s disarmament, a long-term governance plan, and the delivery of needed humanitarian aid in Gaza—are largely stalled.
Perceived success in Venezuela “arguably triggered the overreach that we saw in the decision to begin military operations against Iran without a Plan B if initial objectives were not achieved,” Ulrichsen says.
But the limitations of such rhetoric are most “visible” in the Iran conflict, according to Ulrichsen, who says the U.S. has not been able to “translate rhetoric into gains on the ground.”
Trump has repeatedly predicted that the war would end after the November midterm elections, saying last week that it would end “immediately after” them. He endorsed this belief on Tuesday, as well. Trump initially told reporters that U.S. envoys had held a “very good” three-hour meeting with “mediators of Iran."
“They had a very good meeting, and we'll see how it turns out.

articles.title_zh: AI looms large over Trump-Xi meeting amid deep distrust between US and China | US foreign policy
articles.content_orig:
About two years ago, education entrepreneur Boris But had what he calls a “penny-drop moment” – that, like countless others in China, his company needed to embrace AI before it was made obsolete by it.
His clients, well-off parents looking to send their children to study overseas, had begun arriving in his office reeling off information and opinions gleaned not from rival firms, but from chatbots.
In response, he started developing his own AI study tool, concluding: “If you can’t beat them, join them.”
The pace and quality of AI development in China is second only to the United States, with the two superpowers locked in an intensifying rivalry as the stakes rise with each new model’s capabilities.
Analysts generally agree that frontier, or cutting-edge, US models are still some way ahead of their Chinese counterparts.
But over the last few weeks the mood music from Silicon Valley has been decidedly sombre, as insider after insider has warned of the potential catastrophes that could result from “loss of control” of the most advanced AIs.
And last Saturday Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei pitched a “worldwide pacing of the frontier” – something he said would “require cooperation with China”.
“China is definitely not receptive” to a slowdown on US firms’ terms, though, said Lian Jye Su from technology research group Omdia.
For the government, AI is a “core sovereignty capability”, and Beijing will not want to jeopardise the progress made in closing the gap with US frontier models.
“It sees these calls [for a slowdown] as a bid to lock in US advantage,” said Su.
Amodei made this explicit, mentioning China specifically when arguing it was key “to keep democracies’ AI lead over autocracies as large as possible”.
He advocated for measures including continued export controls to China on advanced chips and machinery – the existence of which some argue already amounts to a forced unilateral “pacing”.
China’s foreign ministry responded to Amodei’s piece by saying “fearmongering, confrontation and vicious competition will only disrupt the process of global AI governance”.
However, several analysts told the Guardian it would be a mistake to assume this suggested a rejection of the broader concerns raised by the essay.
This week China released the third iteration of its AI safety governance framework – a document that functions as a “mapping of the AI risk landscape and roughly what one should do about it”, said Gabriel Wagner, a researcher at Concordia, a Beijing-based AI safety consultancy.
Included in the updates are the risks posed by agents, the cybersecurity threats from frontier models and the issue of recursive self-improvement – an as-yet hypothetical scenario where AI becomes advanced enough to improve itself.
“In many ways, I think there is more common ground than people might assume between what Amodei is saying and what the Chinese government is saying,” said Wagner.
That contrasts with US president Donald Trump, who this week called fears AI could wipe out humanity a “hoax”.
Trump is set to meet counterpart Xi Jinping in Washington next week, with AI expected to make the agenda, though analysts are sceptical a major breakthrough will happen.
The ruling Communist party, finely attuned to risks to its political control, has been proactive in ensuring the new technology has developed within boundaries set by the state.
Centralised authority over critical infrastructure and commercial activity means China is generally better placed than the United States “to address any AI disaster”, said Omdia’s Su.
However, Chinese companies do less voluntary monitoring and evaluation work than US ones, said Leia Wang from the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace (CEIP).
Neither government seems prepared for a loss-of-control incident like those outlined over the last few weeks, she said.
China’s regulation, though, is “iterative … they are quick to adapt and release new measures”, she added.
China has had an algorithm registry since 2022, but warnings on agents released this year suggest a switch in focus “from controlling what AI says to controlling what it does”, per Concordia AI.
Beijing also issued national regulations this year aimed at curbing emotional dependency on companion AIs.
At the same time, AI is being actively encouraged across the economy to promote growth, enshrining this goal in its latest Five Year Plan.
Local governments are offering funding and low rents to companies to help achieve this – entrepreneur But was recently invited to pitch his company, Hampshire Education, to a small city three hours from Shanghai set on establishing a reputation as a tech hub.
Factories across the country’s huge manufacturing base are being encouraged to convert their processes into the AI era.
“Safety and controllability are certainly major concerns, and they are actively discussed,” said a representative for Black Lake Technologies, an industrial agent platform that says it has worked with 40,000 factories globally.
“But in manufacturing, these concerns tend to be much more concrete and operational … what companies care most about is whether the AI is reliable.”
Daily life in China is already highly digitised, with traditionally less discourse around data privacy helping with widespread adoption.
For example, digital health service A-fu, which features AI chatbot versions of prominent doctors trained on real clinical studies, recently hit 150 million users.
“Most people treat AI as an already-useful everyday tool, not an abstract threat, so the practical attitude is to live with it,” said Ni Tao, founding editor of tech website yangtzeer.com.
“There is real anxiety about jobs and misinformation, but it coexists with a strong belief that China must master AI rather than slow down.”

articles.title_zh: US judge blocks deportation of DoorDash driver shot by ICE
articles.content_orig:
US judge blocks deportation of DoorDash driver shot by ICE
A US judge has temporarily blocked the deportation of a Venezuelan man who was shot by immigration agents in Texas, his lawyer says.
Wilber Rafael Garces Perez, 28, is being held in a detention centre with a bullet in his back, according to his lawyer. Judge Orlando Garcia, a Clinton appointee, scheduled a hearing for Garces Perez to appear in court in person next week.
The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) said in a statement that an "illegal alien" had been the subject of a targeted vehicle stop but pushed back against suggestions he had been given inadequate medical care.
The incident comes months after a US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer fatally shot a man in Houston.
Garces Perez's immigration lawyer, Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch, has filed a federal lawsuit for a temporary restraining order to prevent his removal from the country.
Since the judge ordered that her client appear in person on 30 September, he cannot be deported before then, she said.
"For now, we have secured a temporary block on his deportation while his case moves forward," Lincoln-Goldfinch wrote on social media.
"This is an important step, but our work is not over," she wrote. "Wilber still needs appropriate medical care, and we will continue fighting to protect his rights."
The gunshot fractured his clavicle and he is wearing a sling while having "significant swelling and pain," Lincoln-Goldfinch said.
The cause or extent of the loss of movement he experienced has not yet been determined, she said.
A spokesperson for US Attorney's Office in Texas declined to comment on the case.
The ICE agent who shot him - who joined the agency last year - was not wearing a body camera at the time of the shooting, sources told the BBC’s US partner CBS News.
The Austin Police Department released footage from officers responding to the scene, but did not show what led to the incident.
On Tuesday, DHS pushed back against what it called "false narratives" surrounding what had happened, blaming sanctuary cities and media for "spreading lies" and discouraging people from resisting officers and evading arrest.
"Contrary to their claims, this person is an illegal alien who has no legal status to be here and has been given some of the best medical care he's ever received in his life," said DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin in a statement to the BBC.
DHS said the man, whom they did not name, was "the subject of a targeted vehicle stop" and that his work permit expired last year.
"No amount of smears and false narratives will slow down ICE from doing its job by removing dangerous illegal aliens from our communities and making America safe again," Mullin said.
The Austin Police Department, which was not involved in the incident, released dashcam and body camera footage on Tuesday showing its officers at the scene.
It does not show the shooting, but several gunshots can be heard in one dashcam clip, while another shows officers approaching Garces Perez's car and detaining him. At one point, Garces Perez's t-shirt is cut to reveal what appears to be a single gunshot in his back.
Lincoln-Goldfinch previously told the BBC that after being unable to move his arm in the detention facility, Garces Perez was taken back to hospital on Monday evening. He was treated there and has since been returned to the detention facility.
He said he was handcuffed, shackled at the ankles, placed in a waist chain, and handled roughly during his transfer, despite his injury, she said.
Lincoln-Goldfinch added that detention personnel had revoked his communication privileges and moved him from an infirmary into an isolated room with a flat, non-adjustable bed.
In its statement on Tuesday, DHS said Garces Perez had received medical care "around the clock" and denied claims he received no pain medication and was forced to sleep on the floor.
"This alien was released from the hospital and arrived at the detention facility just a few hours later, where he slept on a bed," DHS said.
Texas lawmaker Joaquin Castro, a Democrat, on Tuesday demanded the Venezuelan national's release from detention.
Local and state officials have pushed for an independent investigation into the shooting, which occurred just before on Sunday afternoon.
Hours later, dozens of protesters, some waving the flags of Mexico and Guatemala, gathered at the scene carrying signs demanding that ICE leave the city.
DHS said on Tuesday that ICE "will not be slowing down nor leaving Austin".
The man's lawyer told US media he was making a DoorDash delivery when an unmarked black truck sideswiped his car.
He did not know the truck was an ICE vehicle and made a U-turn, she said. His car was hit again before agents got out and shot him, according to the attorney.

articles.title_orig: ‘I am the code’: Trump clashed with ballroom architect over safety issues
articles.title_zh: ‘I am the code’: Trump clashed with ballroom architect over safety issues
articles.content_orig:
Trump’s ballroom architect quit after president dismissed safety concerns with the design: report
The architect who worked on the preliminary design of President Donald Trump's $400 million White House ballroom stepped down last year after repeatedly raising concerns that the plans violated building safety codes, according to a report.
Trump selected D.C.-based James McCrery II as the lead architect on the project, announced by the White House in July 2025. But a few months later, the classical architect resigned following clashes with the president, according to The Washington Post.
In the weeks prior to leaving the project, McCrery aired concerns about inadequate emergency exits and fire safety measures, according to the outlet. In one reported exchange, the president responded by arguing that the building codes don't apply to White House construction, telling McCrery, "I am the code."
The newspaper obtained documents, including preliminary drawings of the ballroom scrawled with notes in Trump's signature black Sharpie. One of them appeared to mock the architect's concerns over Trump's wishes to increase the size of the ballroom. "James. And you think this is big enough," the note said.
Another note for McCrery written in Sharpie over an image of a White House colonnade said, "James - great look - but Corinthian columns." The president is known to favor the ornate columns.
McCrery, appointed by Trump to the Commission of Fine Arts, did not offer a specific reason for his departure from the project to the Post.
A White House official said that it was "factually false and totally inaccurate" to suggest McCrery left the project over issues with the code, touting him as a "valued member of the initial design team."
The Independent has contacted McCrery's office for further comment.
Trump's White House ballroom project is being overseen by the Executive Residence, a small office that is not required to follow federal rules. Typically, it is responsible for routine repairs to the People's House, entertainment expenses and the purchase of decorative furniture and artwork, not major construction projects, which are usually handled by the General Services Administration or National Park Service.
McCrery left the project on October 20 last year, the week demolition began on the historic East Wing, according to documents reviewed by the newspaper.
His chief concerns with the preliminary design were reportedly that the plans were not up to fire safety codes, ensuring guests can swiftly exit through the main entrance in an emergency, and that alternative exits were "insufficient."
There was reportedly "little in the design" that would prevent a fire from quickly spreading from the kitchen into the event space.
Another major concern was the lack of bathroom stalls for the number of guests. In an early design, the women's bathroom reportedly only had seven stalls.
At a meeting on September 30, White House officials discussed "areas of concern" raised by contractors working on the ballroom. One of the notes reportedly said, "Life safety — big concern."
A White House official said compliance with safety codes has always been a priority and the life safety issues have been addressed and resolved continuously. Addressing McCrery's departure, the official added that a decision was made to move in another direction for the second phase of the project but did not elaborate.
McCrery said that he was "truly grateful" to have worked with Trump on the project in a statement to the Post but did not elaborate on the reason for his departure. "Having completed the earliest designs, I stepped aside and a new firm was engaged," he said.
Trump's ballroom is unpopular with the public and has faced legal challenges, but the president has justified the project due to national security, sharing AI visions for a drone port atop the ballroom.
The Supreme Court in August cleared Trump to continue construction as the legal challenge moves ahead.

articles.title_orig: Taylor Swift Announces ‘The Life of a Showgirl: The Encore’ Album With Four New Songs
articles.title_zh: Taylor Swift Announces ‘The Life of a Showgirl: The Encore’ Album With Four New Songs
articles.content_orig:
No surprise here: “Patient Zero,” the song Taylor Swift announced Tuesday, is not an orphan or a one-off. The pop superstar followed news of the single a day later with her Wednesday morning reveal for a release that includes four new tracks and will also be out this Friday — “The Life of a Showgirl: The Encore.”
A visit to pre-order pages shows that the new songs, besides the already announced “Patient Zero,” are “Cleveland!,” “Pink Clouding” and “Babylon,” listed as tracks 13-16 on the newly expanded version of her 2025 “Showgirl” album.
On social media, Swift wrote, “About a year ago, you guys did a truly unfathomable thing. Something that completely blew my mind… You gave ‘The Life of a Showgirl’ the biggest first week for an album in history. I took a trip to Sweden to celebrate with Max and Shellback, my two collaborators on this album. Really we just wanted to reflect and take in how grateful we were for the moment we were in, but there was a studio there and we did what we do when we feel anything at all: We wrote more songs. I hope you love them, because they were born out of pure gratitude for your exuberance for and celebration of the album we made. ‘The Life of a Showgirl: The Encore’ including four new songs is out on Friday and available to pre-order and save now.”
Swifties had long assumed there would be no deluxe or bonus-filled edition of 2025’s “The Life of a Showgirl” because, at the time, Swift had assured fans that she felt pleased with the exact 12-song configuration she was putting out and did want to augment it with anything she might have left on the cutting room floor. But, as fans now learn, that didn’t preclude coming up with additional material after the fact, which the singer is saying came out in a spontaneous explosion of post-release exhilaration with her two collaborators on that album.
Prior to “Showgirl,” she hadn’t worked with the dynamic duo of Max Martin and Shellback since 2018’s “Reputation,” but clearly the reunion took in a big way.
Eagle-eyed Swifties noted that Swift had quietly teased this project some time ago, by including the phrase “Patient for the encore” to the side of the frame in her music video for the “Showgirl” single “Opalite.”
Much more recently, she had given fans Easter eggs in puzzle form with a pre-taped sketch that aired as part of the Emmys telecast. There; Swift, in character as a “Law & Order: SVU” detective, said, “I think what we’re going to be looking for is hiding in plain sight.” She then stared into the camera and uttered several seeming nonsense phrases or words: “Saccharide. Aries. From the vineyard. North or south.” Fans eventually figured out that if you took the third letter from each of those utterances, they gave up the letters that form the word “encore.”
The announcement of the “Encore” edition also settles another point of trivia that had come up when Swift revealed the “Patient Zero” single was imminent on Tuesday. Many pointed out that Swift was not lately in the habit of releasing a stand-alone single ahead of an album actually coming out; the last time she had done so was with “Me!” being released months ahead of “Lover” in 2019. Now that everyone knows the “Encore” collection is coming out the same hour as the single, it’s clear she’s not breaking with that recent pattern after all.
The new release features cover photography by the team of fashion photographers Mert Alas and Marcus Piggott, continuing the imagery they created ffor the original “Showgirl” album.
No physical release has been announced for the expanded project, which hits DSPs as Thursday night turns into Friday morning. The streaming service Apple Music does show the track list as being broken down into Disc 1 (the original 12 tracks) and Disc 2 (the four newly released songs), but it’s unclear if that augurs for a two-disc vinyl or CD edition. Spotify has the 16 tracks listed in a single running order.
For now, the release of the four “Showgirl” addenda puts to bed previous widespread conjecture that Swift was certain to put out “Taylor Swift (Taylor’s Version)” this fall to celebrate the 20th anniversary of her debut album. But setting that aside for newly written songs is a tradeoff most fans will be happy with. So, “Our Song (Middle Aged Version)” can wait.

articles.title_zh: Dolly Parton estate in feud with nephew over alleged ‘warfare’ threats
articles.content_orig:
The estate of the late Dolly Parton is involved in a dispute with the country star’s nephew and former head of security, and has filed for a restraining order against him amid allegations of threats.
Bryan Seaver was responsible for Parton’s security, and was tasked with announcing her death on 25 August with a video, “something Dolly asked of me years ago”, he said.
But since the singer died, her estate, which is run by Parton’s manager Danny Nozell, has reportedly fired Seaver from his security job, and has now alleged that he made “relentless” threats against Nozell and others.
According to Billboard, the lawsuit filed in a Tennessee court reads: “These were not ordinary workplace disputes or heated words; they were deliberate threats from a self-proclaimed heavily armed, former security operative with a military-contractor background. Many of [Parton’s staff members] are now afraid to come to work or have resigned entirely because they do not feel safe.”
Seaver is alleged to have written to a lawyer for Parton, “I’m a killer”, and separately told Nozell: “I’m literally an international arms dealer and mercenary. All I do is warfare. Everyone needs to be worried about what I might do.” He is also alleged to have claimed that he made a $27m arms and ammunition deal with Haiti.
He allegedly claimed he would “set up a podcast dedicated to ruining Dolly’s brand partnerships and telling the violations these people have done on us. It’s going to be great. Or fucking pay me.”
Seaver repeated some of those claims in comments to TMZ while defending his actions, saying: “I am a career soldier and military contractor and do conduct arms deals for foreign governments. I am a security professional and I am a killer. However, nothing in this lawsuit were threats and most of the comments I stand by.”
Regarding the messages to Nozell, Seaver said: “I was talking frankly in a private way with Danny who I thought was my friend and he fancies himself a gangster. A lot of these messages are two guys having rage talk and crying on the phone together while we were grieving.”
In another message, Seaver reportedly said: “I’m going to spend the next times I have on earth ratfucking anyone that has ever betrayed my family.”
Speaking to TMZ, Seaver said of that comment: “I was talking about people that have done bad to Dolly in business – a specific company that scared her and intimated her. Those comments were about specific, horrible business partners that have done wrong to her and I stand by that.”
Seaver’s security contract was terminated on 15 September, with a leaked termination letter saying the decision was made “for the protection of the trust and beneficiaries as a whole”, though it reassured Seaver it was “not a termination of your personal interest in the trust”.
Seaver put out a statement after the termination, saying: “We remain unshakably resolved to fulfil her final directive to protect her family, and we refuse to be intimidated by those whose actions we believe are being taken in bad faith and with the intent to profit from the life of someone who willingly gave so much.”
The chancery court in Nashville will now consider the restraining order filing. The Guardian has contacted Seaver and lawyers for Parton’s estate for further comment.
Parton left behind considerable financial assets: not only her songbook featuring hits such as 9 to 5, but also a broad business empire including the entertainment resort Dollywood in Tennessee.
She had no children, and her husband, Carl, died in 2025, but she is survived by other family members including six siblings and an uncle. Seaver is the son of her sister Cassie.

articles.title_zh: Xiaomi’s new 18 Pro phones improve on Samsung’s privacy display
articles.content_orig:
Xiaomi’s new 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max launched in China today, and feature a more flexible take on the privacy display tech introduced this year on Samsung’s Galaxy S26 Ultra. They combine it with returning rear screens, two 200-megapixel cameras, and both of Qualcomm’s new Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 chips. A global launch is confirmed for later this year — especially welcome since last year’s 17 Pro phones skipped international markets.
Xiaomi’s new 18 Pro phones improve on Samsung’s privacy display
An international launch is coming later this year.
The two 18 Pro phones look similar to the 17 Pros, with similar compact displays built around the rear cameras, capable of displaying notifications, taking selfies, playing simple games, and more.
The bigger changes are to the front screen, which is now equipped with hardware-level privacy features much like the S26 Ultra’s. Xiaomi’s implementation looks smarter than Samsung’s though: When you activate it for a specific app, it will not only turn on when that app is opened, but apply to notifications, floating windows, and split-screen views, without affecting the rest of the display. Location-based triggers allow you to set it to turn on when you reach work, or off when you come home, with smart triggers for when it detects locations like airports or elevators. It can also use the selfie camera to detect prying eyes and suggest activating the privacy mode.
The two phones differ in size, with a 6.4-inch display on the Pro and 6.9 inches for the Pro Max. Battery varies accordingly: 7,000mAh or 8,500mAh respectively, using a high 32 percent silicon content. The other difference between the two is the chipset, with the Snapdragon 8 Gen 6 Elite in the Pro and the Extreme version in the Pro Max, though differences between the two chips are slight.
Cameras are led by a 200-megapixel main camera using a large 1/1.28-inch-type sensor (the Light Fusion 960 in the Pro, and 960L in the Pro Max, though they seem similar). A 200-megapixel, 75mm telephoto joins it, the same on both phones, using Samsung’s 1/1.56-inch HP5 sensor and with a minimum focus distance of 12cm. A 50-megapixel ultrawide completes the trio.
Xiaomi’s launch follows similar announcements this week for the Vivo X500 and Oppo Find X10 flagships. The two 18 Pro phones start from ¥5,999 (about $900), and join the 18 Fold in Xiaomi’s new flagship lineup, but we’re still waiting for the regular Xiaomi 18 and the 18 Ultra, likely to appear next spring. An international launch for at least one 18 Pro phone will come later this year, though we’re still waiting to hear if the Fold will ever leave China.

articles.title_orig: First Thing: Trump addresses UN with mixture of boasts, threats and jibes
articles.title_zh: First Thing: Trump addresses UN with mixture of boasts, threats and jibes
articles.content_orig:
Good morning. Donald Trump has used the platform of the UN general assembly in New York to threaten to “annihilate the Islamic republic” of Iran, “and do it quickly”. He called on countries to unite to isolate Tehran and bring down global energy prices.
Despite his bombastic rhetoric, Trump also said Iranian officials held three hours of talks with the US special envoy Steve Witkoff on the sidelines of the meeting. Witkoff said he felt very good about the meeting, the first such contact since the US vice-president, JD Vance, met an Iranian delegation in Switzerland in June. A senior Iranian official also indicated that Iran was prepared to reopen the strait of Hormuz within a week.
What else did Trump say at the UN? The president doubled down on his defence of AI development, saying warnings about runaway agents were a “hoax”; announced the US would build new military bases in Greenland; attacked the international criminal court as a “rogue organisation”; and prompted the Cuba’s delegation to stage a walkout when he described the country as a “failed state”.
Did he continue his attacks on US media networks? Trump scolded a CNN anchor for covering him at the UN, saying “I’m surprised that CNN is here covering me. You should not be here covering me. You said you weren’t going to cover me.” Last week, the president announced he was banning CNN, Politico and MS Now from the White House.
Follow UN proceedings live today here.
Republican calls for Senate investigation of Trump Jr wedding paid for by Russian oligarch
A Republican senator has accused Donald Trump Jr of corruption and demanded a Senate investigation into revelations that a Russian oligarch bankrolled part of his recent wedding in the Bahamas.
John Curtis, of Utah, wrote to the leaders of the US Senate judiciary committee on Tuesday, urging them to subpoena Trump Jr over his business dealings, his relationships with foreign individuals, gifts he has received – and any occasions where his connection to his father, Donald Trump, “was invoked or understood to provide value”.
Where else is the president seeing dissent from Republicans? Another prominent Florida Republican has publicly distanced himself from Trump, days after María Elvira Salazar called out the president’s immigration-enforcement policy targeting law-abiding undocumented immigrants. Byron Donalds, the Republican nominee for governor in November’s midterm elections, launched an updated campaign website on Tuesday that was stripped of almost every mention of Trump.
Mississippi grand jury decides not to charge anyone in death of Nolan Wells
A grand jury made a unanimous decision to not bring criminal charges against anyone in the mysterious death of Nolan Wells, a Mississippi teenager who died after a boat outing with friends on 4 July.
Wells’s case drew national attention, with many speculating about what happened and suspecting that the 18-year-old’s disappearance and death may have been racially motivated. Wells, who was Black while the friends with whom he was last seen were white, was also the only friend in the group who did not return from the trip that day.
Hayden Panettiere’s cause of death confirmed as fentanyl overdose
Hayden Panettiere died from a fentanyl overdose, according to the Greenville county coroner’s office. Medical examiners said there were “no signs of trauma” and “the manner of death has been ruled accident”. Panettiere was in her South Carolina apartment with her boyfriend, Brian Hickerson, and his brother Zach when she died on August 16.
Panettiere, known for her roles in television series including Heroes and Nashville, began acting at just 11 months old. After her death, her father released a statement, saying: “She was an incredible light and a force of nature who brought immeasurable love and joy to all who knew her – and to the millions who watched her onscreen.”
Ella Langley’s hit song Choosin’ Texas has set a new record, spending 23 weeks at the top of the Billboard Hot 100, unseating Mariah Carey’s All I Want for Christmas Is You, which topped the charts for 22 weeks.
An US F-16 fighter jet in western Germany crashed on Tuesday, the US military said, adding that one pilot had ejected safely.
DoorDash said it would pay $131.5m to settle a New York City government investigation that found the food delivery company underpaid or waited too long to pay workers.
‘Looksmaxxing’ influencer Clavicular has been charged with rape and drug offenses in Massachusetts. The 20-year-old, whose real name is Braden Eric Peters, has been scheduled for a 14 October arraignment.
Qantas says travellers will be able to fly between Sydney and New York in just 18 hours from mid-2028 when the airline launches its second ultra long-haul route.
Stat of the day: Trump made more than 1,000 stock trades in July worth up to $270m
The president made more than 440 purchases and 700 sales despite voter anger over elected officials trading stocks.
Well Actually: Get tested and talk to your partner – how to have safer sex after age 50
We are long past the era when sex was for young married couples trying for children and nobody else. Amanda Zuckerman Klarsfeld has compiled this thoughtful selection of advice for older lovers.
Don’t miss this: Why public transport in global cities is slowing to a crawl – visualised
The UK capital’s iconic red buses have a problem: they are getting slower. And it isn’t just an issue in London, but a growing worldwide problem for transit networks, with worrying implications for the poorest in society. Our visuals team have put together this rich explainer to explore why.
… or this: Will anyone topple soccer boss Infantino?
Since Fifa abandoned its controversial World Cup sell-off plan last month, causing deep divisions among the global administrators of soccer, the governing body’s president, Gianni Infantino, has continued to lobby for re-election. Matt Hughes analyses how he is trying to cling on after the debacle.
Climate check: Huge El Niño projected to cause 450,000 deaths in next six months
More than 450,000 people are projected to die from the additional heat brought by the super El Niño in the next six months, according to estimates by climate scientists. The toll is on top of the early deaths resulting from temperatures already driven up by the climate crisis. It will strike across the globe, including the US. Many further deaths are expected from the droughts, wildfires and flooding that El Niños bring.

My colleague Sammy Gecsoyler has taken up pilates, and has written this very funny account of his month’s journey to better fitness and health.

articles.title_orig: Defending Trump media ban, DOJ cites national security and says White House access is a ‘privilege’
articles.title_zh: Defending Trump media ban, DOJ cites national security and says White House access is a ‘privilege’
articles.content_orig:
The Department of Justice said in a court filing late Tuesday that President Donald Trump has the right to ban media outlets CNN, MSNOW and Politico from the White House, calling their access a “privilege” and citing national security concerns.
The filing urges a federal judge not to block the ban, ahead of a hearing Wednesday on the news organizations’ request for a temporary order restoring their access.
The Trump administration argues that the ban does not violate First Amendment protections on press freedom. “Access to the White House is a privilege—not a right,” the DOJ says in the filing.
It contends that the three news outlets had “failed to maintain basic minimum ‘standards of professionalism and decorum expected of those given access to the White House Complex,’ including, “publishing sensitive or classified information,” wrote DOJ Attorney Michael Velchik.
The DOJ said the three news organizations were sent individual letters from the White House Press Office earlier Tuesday laying out the reasoning for the revocation of their passes, and citing a “non-exhaustive list of reporting incidents” the White House said it had found “threatened national security and spread falsehoods.”
The letters cite stories on construction details related to the East Wing bunker, funding for the White House ballroom, munitions stockpiles impacted by the Iran war and sanctions against Russia.
The outlets did not immediately respond to overnight requests for comment from NBC News on the filing’s claims.
The letters give the news organizations a deadline of 5 p.m. on Friday to “contest this initial decision.” If the deadline is missed “this initial decision will be final,” they say.
Rubio defends White House media outlet ban
The decision to ban CNN, Politico and MS NOW came Friday via a Truth Social post, where Trump wrote that he was “proud to announce” the ban from the White House “effective immediately.”
He said the decision was “a result of their constant “reporting” FAKE NEWS! Media Outlets shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they’re covering the President of the United States, the Trump Administration, or the United States of America.” He added: “Other Fake News Media Outlets to follow.”
Journalists from the three outlets, including MS NOW reporter Akayla Gardner, CNN’s Betsy Klein and Politico’s Cheyenne Haslett, subsequently found their access passes deactivated and their White House press credentials confiscated.
First Amendment experts and the White House Correspondents’ Association called the turning away of credentialed reporters unconstitutional.
CNN, Politico and MS NOW filed their lawsuit Monday arguing that the president’s move violated the defendants’ due process rights and First Amendment protections for newsgathering and speech.
The three outlets said they were filing the lawsuit “to protect our First Amendment rights and defend the principle that the government does not decide what the press reports or publishes.”
U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly, who was appointed by Trump in 2017, will preside over the hearing Wednesday. He will evaluate the outlets’ request to issue a temporary restraining order blocking enforcement of the ban and restoring reporters’ hard passes to access White House grounds.
Kelly ruled against Trump in a similar case back in 2018, when the White House withdrew credentials from reporter Jim Acosta, who was then with CNN.
On Tuesday, Trump remarked that he would “probably” let journalists from CNN, MS NOW and Politico back into the White House if a court rules against his decision to ban the media outlets from the White House grounds.
Later that day, during his address to the United Nations’ General Assembly in New York, Trump told CNN reporter Kaitlan Collins: “You shouldn’t be here ... You said you weren’t going to cover me.” Collins responded that CNN never said it was not going to cover Trump, and that while it had been banned from the White House it was credentialed by the U.N. as usual.
The solidarity among TV networks has been swift, as they refused to provide TV pool coverage of the president’s activities this week, resulting in quiet mics and a lack of photographs of Trump’s official activities.
Pool coverage is when one network attends an event and then distributes information and media, such as video footage and audio, to other outlets. The system has been recognized by administrations from both parties for decades, and the coverage is used by pool members and subscribers, which includes outlets like Newsmax, One America News Network, C-SPAN and international outlets.
Print and radio pools are still in place, and TV pools for events for other parts of the administration will continue. Individual TV networks, including NBC News, continue to provide coverage of White House events that are open to the press, outside of the pool. Outside of events, NBC News reporters continue to report on the administration’s activities.

articles.title_orig: Nearly 10% of borrowers opted for riskier mortgages last week, as rates soared over 7%
articles.title_zh: Nearly 10% of borrowers opted for riskier mortgages last week, as rates soared over 7%
articles.content_orig:
Mortgage rates soared to the highest level since 2024 last week, causing loan demand to fall back again and more borrowers to opt for riskier loans. Total application volume decreased 1.5% from the previous week, according to the Mortgage Bankers Association's seasonally adjusted index.
The average contract interest rate for 30-year fixed-rate mortgages with conforming loan balances, $832,750 or less, increased to 7.12% from 6.97%, with points rising to 0.73 from 0.72, including the origination fee, for loans with a 20% down payment.
Applications to refinance a home loan dropped 3% for the week and were 62% lower than the same week one year ago. That was the lowest level since February 2025. The 30-year fixed loan was 78 basis points, or more than three-quarters of a percentage point lower, at the same time last year.
Applications for a mortgage to purchase a home fell 1% for the week and were 11% lower year over year. The fall housing market, usually the second busiest compared with spring, is now underway, but real estate agents are already noting a sharp pullback due to higher rates. Buyers and current homeowners are also searching for savings anywhere they can find them, even in riskier, adjustable-rate loans.
"With fixed rates much higher, more borrowers opted for ARMs, with the ARM share reaching 9.8%, as rates for 5/1 ARMs were more than a percentage point lower than those for fixed rate loans," said Mike Fratantoni, senior vice president and chief economist at the MBA.
The ARM share of applications the week before last was just 8.4%. During the first years of the pandemic, when rates were hitting multiple record lows, the ARM share was barely 3%. ARMs can carry a fixed rate for up to 10 years but will adjust either higher or lower depending on where the market is when that term is up.
Mortgage rates moved slightly lower to start this week, according to a separate survey from Mortgage News Daily, as the price of oil fell and bond yields moved lower as a result.

Powerful El Nino could cause more than 450,000 deaths, scientists say
Heaviest toll expected in poorer countries, already struggling with food insecurity and high energy costs, report says.
More than 450,000 people are projected to die from additional heat due to the unusually strong El Nino event over the next six months, according to a research report.
The projection, published on Wednesday by the University of Chicago’s Climate Impact Lab, runs to February 2027 and compares estimates of heat-related deaths that could be attributed to El Nino with the level expected in a typical year.

- list 2 of 3US records hottest summer in 132 years

Researchers estimate that global land temperatures could climb by about 1.2 degrees Celsius (2.1 degrees Fahrenheit), with extremely hot days 44 percent more frequent than in an average year.
Developing nations and Africa’s Sahel region are expected to be hit disproportionately hard.
The report projected about 66,800 additional deaths across the Sahel, with Nigeria having the highest projected toll of any single country at 31,400, ahead of Indonesia at 19,300 and Sudan at 17,600.
Elsewhere, the Philippines, Vietnam, Thailand and Cambodia are forecast to see a combined 19,400 extra deaths, with 15,800 projected in India and 13,300 in Brazil.
Michael Greenstone, cofounder of the lab and co-author of the study, said the findings show heat poses the greatest threat where temperatures are already high and incomes relatively low.
“If you’re already in a hot place, the extra couple of degrees are going to be much more dangerous,” he said.
Richer places tend to have better access to air conditioning, steady water supplies and health services, he added.
Greenstone said the heat risk was likely to outlast the El Nino itself, with repercussions stretching into next summer.
Abhiyant Tiwari, who specialises in heat at NRDC India, told The Associated Press news agency that the projections should spur action.
Funding and delivery remain weak points, he said, even in India, which has sound plans on paper.
“The real measure of our preparedness is not how many heat warnings we issue, but how effectively we protect people and reduce preventable deaths,” he said.
This year’s El Nino began developing in June and is expected to be one of the strongest ever. Experts say the natural weather pattern, which occurs cyclically, is being “supercharged” by climate change.
In early September, the United Nations’ weather agency reported a 100 percent likelihood that El Nino will continue through February 2027. But researchers say its dangers could linger into mid-2027.

articles.title_orig: An ancient wall discovered beneath a Paris hotel could confirm the city's origins: "Major breakthrough"
articles.title_zh: An ancient wall discovered beneath a Paris hotel could confirm the city's origins: "Major breakthrough"
articles.content_orig:
An ancient wall discovered beneath a Paris hotel could confirm the city's origins: "Major breakthrough"
An ancient wall discovered beneath Paris was described as a "major breakthrough" on Wednesday by France's culture ministry, with the archaeological find possibly confirming the location of the city's original settlement.
A roughly 65-foot wall dating from the Gallo-Roman period was discovered in Paris this summer beneath a hotel on the Île de la Cité, a stone's throw from Notre Dame Cathedral in the heart of the City of Light.
The stone-and-wood find is thought to be a fragment of the ramparts of Lutetia — the ancient name for Paris — built by the Gallic Parisii tribe which lived along the river Seine in the Iron Age.
The Île de la Cité has traditionally been regarded as the center of Lutetia, but a rival theory, backed by archaeological research, contends that it was in Nanterre, a suburb to the west.
"We may be looking at one of the most important remains ever discovered for understanding Gallic Lutetia," Culture Minister Catherine Pegard said in a statement from her ministry.
"Scientific caution still requires that we verify its function and its chronology, but the convergence of evidence is particularly remarkable at this stage," she added.
Lutetia was first mentioned in book seven of Roman leader Julius Caesar's "Gallic Wars" series, where it was said to be on an island in the river Seine — a vague description that has given rise to many theories about its location.
The wall, uncovered in the course of excavations beneath the Hotel-Dieu, also bears traces of fire, which may correspond to Caesar's account that the Gauls set fire to their town before the Battle of Lutetia against the Romans.
Through carbon dating technology, the charred evidence is estimated to date from 10-200 B.C., the ministry said in its statement — a timeframe that includes the Battle of Lutetia in 52 B.C.
The Île de la Cite, home to Notre Dame cathedral, is the largest island in the river Seine in the Paris region and became the center of the Roman settlement of Lutetia.
Notre Dame itself has yielded numerous archaeological finds. In June, officials announced the discovery of multiple artifacts, including a fourth-century coin and mysterious inscriptions.
In 2022, several tombs and a sarcophagus likely dating from the 14th century were uncovered by archaeologists at the cathedral.
The news of the ancient wall comes less than a year after a massive prehistoric stone wall was found in the sea off the coast of France near the Île de Sein.

articles.title_orig: Discord re-launches age verification following backlash over privacy concerns
articles.title_zh: Discord re-launches age verification following backlash over privacy concerns
articles.content_orig:
Discord re-launches age verification following backlash over privacy concerns
Platform adds alternative methods that do not require video selfies or ID to verify age
Discord has re-launched its age verification process for all users, introducing alternative methods that do not require video selfies or ID.
In an update posted yesterday, Discord co-founder and chief technology officer Stanislav Vishnevskiy stated that users can verify their age using credit cards, the Apple App Store, Google Play Store, Google Wallet, or AgeKey (which does not share personal or private data).
"By launching a global approach with non-biometric options, we're getting ahead of laws that might ask us to implement something less privacy-focused," said Vishnevskiy.
"The decisions policymakers make now will shape how platforms advance both teen safety and privacy for years to come, and I encourage people to make their perspectives heard where they live."
In February, Discord announced that age verification would be required for all users starting in March.
The rollout was postponed to the second half of 2026 due to privacy concerns. At the time, Vishnevskiy acknowledged that Discord "should have provided more detail about [its] intentions and how the process works."
In its latest update, Discord said it would "publicly document every third-party age assurance vendor and make it clear who each vendor is," which it has done since and can be accessed here.
Discord has also published its age group estimation methodology and released its first age assurance data in the 2026 Transparency Report, which includes information from the UK and Australia launches.
"Previously, I said trust is earned through actions, not posts," said Vishnevskiy. "This launch is where you hold us to that. We'll get some things wrong, but you can judge us on how we respond: how accurate the age group estimation gets, how fast we fix bad calls, and whether we keep publishing the data so you don't have to take my word for it. That's how we earn your trust."
Discord's age verification automatically assigns users to an age group based on account age or associated servers. It does not review messages, calls, or other content.
There are three age groups: Adult (18+), Teen (13 to 17), and Unconfirmed.
New accounts are automatically unconfirmed until Discord has enough data to determine an age group. Users who do not verify their age can continue to use Discord with limitations while the platform determines a group to place them in, though they can verify their age in user settings.

Trump meets US-backed Venezuelan president for first time since Maduro seized
US President Donald Trump has held talks with Venezuela's interim President Delcy Rodríguez at the UN General Assembly, their first face-to-face meeting since the White House backed her to take over the South American country's government.
Rodríguez succeeded Nicolás Maduro shortly after US forces conducted a raid on the Venezuelan capital Caracas and seized him.
The pair met a few kilometres from the New York jail where Maduro is awaiting trial for drug trafficking and other charges.
Rodríguez said they discussed "advancing a cooperation agenda in strategic areas such as energy, mining, and security".
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio and White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles also attended the meeting.
Rodríguez's government has signed an agreement allowing the US to control more than 65 billion barrels of its oil - more than a fifth of the country's reserves. It grants a US-led company 100-year concessions over 17 oilfields in Venezuela.
Trump previously called it "the biggest oil deal in world history".
During his address to the UN on Monday, Trump said the US and Venezuela control "more than 60%" of the world's oil, adding: "To the victor belong the spoils."
Rodríguez is due to address the UN on Wednesday.
She previously served as vice-president to Maduro and was sanctioned by the US in 2018, but the measures were lifted in April this year.
She was sworn in as interim president by Venezuela's National Assembly days after the US raid with the White House's blessing.
Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado has repeatedly been barred from re-entering the country.

articles.title_orig: Trump-Xi meeting: Why China's self-sufficiency changes the calculus
articles.title_zh: Trump-Xi meeting: Why China's self-sufficiency changes the calculus
articles.content_orig:
BEIJING — The trade deficit that escalated tensions between China and the U.S. in recent years has yet to shrink significantly, and the world's second-largest economy faces deep challenges. But China's efforts to build up self-sufficiency have reduced the threat to its domestic market from global trade developments.
U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping are expected to meet this week for their second in-person summit of the year. U.S. concerns about artificial intelligence have gained prominence in the days ahead of the meeting.
But the best that businesses are hoping for is an extension of a trade truce reached last fall. Even then, tariffs have done little to dent America's appetite for Chinese goods.
While an escalation in trade tensions last April briefly sent the U.S. trade deficit with China to its lowest level since 2017, surging demand for AI-related parts have helped send it higher again so far this year, according to China Customs data accessed through Wind Information.
And even as the U.S. has diversified away from China, it's hard for the world to shake its dependence on the Asian country.
Asia still accounts for more than 60% of U.S. imports, the same as before "Liberation Day," pointed out Jens Eskelund, president of the European Chamber of Commerce in China.
He estimated between half and three-quarters of container traffic from China to Southeast Asia subsequently heads on to other destinations.
That's all sped up the pace at which the world relies on China-made goods.
Eskelund said he previously expected China to account for 40% of global container exports in the year 2030 — but the milestone was reached this summer.
How did the world get here?
"Probably the China shock only really started in 2022, because I think everything was distorted by the pandemic," Eskelund said. "China was first in the pandemic, and first out of the pandemic, and for that reason China actually could allow its exchange rate to rise, and export prices to rise.
"China could do that because China was the only game in town," he said.
China's real estate market began its downturn in 2022, dragging down domestic demand. Chinese companies ramped up global expansion, and exports.
"There is a direct, perfect correlation between the drop in export prices and the acceleration in export in volume terms," Eskelund said.
U.S. tech companies' buildout of data centers to power AI has supported demand for Chinese goods.
But think tank CF40 estimated that for the first time this year, AI-related exports fell significantly in August from a year ago.
Macquarie's chief China economist Larry Hu last week also pointed out that the recent performance of the PHLX Semiconductor Index — which he said tends to be predictive of how China's high-tech exports will grow in the next six months — "does not bode well for China's export outlook over the next year."
Still, economists don't expect China's policymakers to do much.
Within tech-related manufacturing, industrial robot output rose by 34.6% year-on-year in August, while smartphone output fell by 22.3%.
"Because there are always high-flying subsectors for the government to point to, policymakers do not appear to feel much urgency to introduce additional easing measures, absent a sharp deterioration in the labor market," Goldman Sachs' chief China economist Hui Shan said in a Sept. 20 report.
She pointed out house prices have already seen a 30% decline over a six-year timeline, typical of historical large-scale property downturns in other parts of the world. "Weak labor markets and still-falling rents are likely to prolong the downturn in many parts of China," she added.
The number of loss-making companies is also on the rise, accounting for 24% of industrial firms in China in 2025.
The economic slowdown has only pushed companies in China to compete even more fiercely with each other, and their foreign rivals.
The American Chamber of Commerce in Shanghai said this month that three-quarters of members responding to a survey saw Chinese rivals as more advanced, and that the perceived gap in product quality narrowed by 6 percentage points from last year.
For the first time since 2022, domestic competition has surpassed geopolitical tensions as the top challenge for members, the chamber said.
It's all spilling over internationally, as European Union officials are starting to follow the U.S. in scrutiny of China-origin exports. EU Trade Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič, who urged "tangible results" from China on trade by October, is expected to travel to Beijing next month.
The European Union has the largest trade deficit with China of any economy, Eskelund pointed out.
In addition to competing through lower-cost goods, Chinese companies have also come to dominate global supply chains for critical minerals. This also supports Beijing's self-sufficiency goals.
"There's no sense in which China's strategy seems to be at all dependent on actions that the rest of the world might take," said Chad Bown, senior fellow at the U.S.-based Peterson Institute for International Economics.
It's "this strategy of a one-way dependence of the rest of the world on China that it's going to weaponize."
—CNBC's Anniek Bao contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Trump’s midterm woes deepen amid worsened economic backdrop: CNN poll
articles.title_zh: Trump’s midterm woes deepen amid worsened economic backdrop: CNN poll
articles.content_orig:
With President Donald Trump at record unpopularity, Republicans are facing an even bleaker midterm political landscape than they did eight years ago, a new CNN poll conducted by SSRS finds.
Nationally, voters say they prefer Democratic candidates over Republicans by an eight-point margin – slightly more modest than their 12-point advantage in CNN’s September polling ahead of the 2018 midterms in Trump’s first presidency.
But Trump is even more unpopular than he was in 2018, and the economic backdrop has worsened considerably. In his first term, Trump saw net-positive ratings on the economy, which Americans largely saw as thriving. Now, just 27% of Americans approve of Trump on the economy, down 22 points from 2018. And 28% call economic conditions good – a drop of 41 points.
The issue has risen in prominence: Two-thirds of registered voters call the economy “extremely important” to their vote, higher than in the autumn before either of the past two midterms. And, in a shift from recent trends, Americans say they agree more with Democrats than Republicans when it comes to the issue.
That leaves a midterm electorate in which the president’s supporters are largely tepid, while his opponents are furious. In a midterm high for an incumbent president dating back to the George W. Bush era, 44% of registered voters say they view their congressional vote as a message of opposition to Trump. Just 19%, by contrast, say their vote will be a message of support for the president.
At the same time, the public remains split on what a Democratic congressional victory might mean for the cost of living in the US, or their own financial situation.
Support for Trump continues to erode
Overall, just one-third of Americans now approve of Trump’s job performance, the continuation of a steady decline throughout his second term. That’s on par with the 34% he saw in July, but marks a numeric low in either term of his presidency.
Only 13% now say they strongly approve of his performance, another career low. Just 24% say he has the right priorities, and a scant 20% approve of his handling of inflation.
Two-thirds of Americans say Trump has worsened economic conditions in the country, and majorities say that the war in Iran, as well as new tariffs, have had a negative effect on their own finances. By contrast, few say they’re seeing benefits from Trump policies like changes to the tax law, or the establishment of Trump Accounts for children born during his second term. Most Americans also call increased gas prices a financial hardship for their household – and though only about one-quarter call that hardship severe, the public remains dubious that Trump has any plan to address the issue.
A 57% majority of Americans say they feel uncertain about their own finances, with nearly half expressing stress about their financial future – a sentiment that’s particularly acute among younger adults. Just 31% of Americans say they feel hope and 23% that they feel security, down 8 and 7 points respectively from spring. More than one-third aren’t confident about maintaining their current standard of living, worse than the numbers at the tail end of the Great Recession.
While Republicans haven’t deserted Trump, relatively few remain enthusiastic about the current state of his presidency. Only 35% say they strongly approve of him, down from 66% in September 2018. In the latest poll, 50% of Republicans disapprove of Trump’s handling of inflation, 59% say the Iran war has hurt their finances, and nearly half say he’s worsened or had no effect on economic conditions.
Democrats are fired up for the midterm, but the public’s expectations for a Democratic Congress aren’t high
Overall, voters say, 49% to 41%, that they’d support a Democratic candidate over a Republican candidate in their congressional district. Democratic and Democratic-leaning registered voters are 16 points likelier than GOP-aligned voters to say they’re extremely motivated to vote this year.
Among the full public, anger at Trump and deep dissatisfaction with the status quo are paired with real skepticism about the prospects of a Democratic-controlled Congress.
Both congressional Democrats and congressional Republicans are deeply – and about equally – unpopular, with about one-quarter of Americans approving.
And while Americans say by a 10-point margin that a Democratic-controlled Congress would have a positive effect on health care policy, they’re closely split on whether a change in power would be more positive or negative when it comes to the cost of living in the US, their own finances, corruption, or foreign policy.
But the Democrats are nevertheless seen as the lesser of two evils on a crucial issue: They lead the GOP by 7 points as the party Americans say is closest to their own views on the economy. Over the past four years, this is both by far the best number for Democrats and the worst for Republicans on the topic.
A 68% majority of voters call the economy “extremely important” to their vote, topping a list of more than 10 issues. That’s far higher than the 59% in fall 2022 or 44% in fall 2018 who called the issue extremely important.
The poll finds that elections themselves, election integrity and voting rights are also at the forefront of many partisans’ minds as Trump continues his efforts to reshape or cast doubt on parts of the voting system, with 61% calling the issue extremely important. Majorities also say that inflation and health care are extremely important, while other hot-button issues – including data centers and AI, abortion, and policies around gender identity and trans people – don’t register as deeply.
Voters’ decisions, though, aren’t always down to which issues they find most important – more than half of voters say that other factors will be more important in their vote for Congress this year. And in this year where discontent with Washington is at the forefront of many voters’ minds, about a third say their votes will be primarily driven by which party will control the House of Representatives, including almost 4 in 10 of the most motivated voters.
CNN’s Jennifer Agiesta, Edward Wu and Isabelle LaBianco contributed to this report.
The CNN poll was conducted by SSRS online and by telephone September 16-17 among a random national sample of 1,206 adults, including 867 registered voters. Results for the full sample have a margin of sampling error of plus or minus 3.5 percentage points; it is 4.1 points among registered voters.

articles.title_orig: Poll: Canadians and Americans agree, Trump was in the wrong with trade war
articles.title_zh: Poll: Canadians and Americans agree, Trump was in the wrong with trade war
articles.content_orig:
It’s become an article of faith for trade hardliners in both parties that a protectionist agenda is a guaranteed pathway to building support among working-class voters. But now that President Donald Trump is testing that theory in practice, it is largely flopping on the campaign trail.
Trump has pursued the most confrontational trade agenda of any president since at least William McKinley at the end of the 19th century, and by the estimation of some historians, even Thomas Jefferson around its beginning.
But even in heavily blue-collar states and House districts that were long believed to be the most receptive to a protectionist agenda, Democrats almost uniformly have been comfortable this year running against the Trump tariffs, while Republicans have struggled to defend them. Even Democrats who are deeply skeptical of free trade agreements — like Ohio Senate candidate Sherrod Brown and Brian Poindexter, the ironworker running against Rep. Max Miller for an Ohio House seat — have been unreserved in condemning the Trump tariffs. Polls by CNN and other media organizations consistently show that far more Americans believe the tariffs have hurt rather than helped their financial bottom line — and that consensus extends even to working-class white voters without a four-year college degree.
All this marks a fundamental shift in the politics of trade that could loosen Trump’s hold on the working-class voters at the core of his coalition — and allow Democrats this fall to recover some of the ground they have lost in blue-collar and rural places. Trump’s skepticism about the North American Free Trade Agreement and other moves to lower trade barriers clearly helped power his historic gains in blue-collar communities during his initial 2016 race and his first presidential term. But his sweeping second-term tariffs — which exceed even the wish lists that other protectionist presidential candidates have put forward since the 1970s — appear to be bleeding Republican support, even in those working-class places. “Everyone else talked about it, but Trump did it,” says Douglas Holtz-Eakin, president of the American Action Forum, a center-right think tank. “And voters are like: ‘no thanks.’”
The most protectionist president in modern history
For decades, a steady procession of presidential hopefuls in both parties had offered a tough-on-trade message and an assortment of policies to restrict imports. That list extends from Republican John Connally in 1980 to Democrats Walter Mondale and Richard Gephardt in the 1980s to GOP insurgent Patrick J. Buchanan and independent candidate Ross Perot in the 1990s.
But before Trump, none of them won the presidency — and with it the ability to implement a protectionist agenda. Presidents of both parties have often provided some protection to American industries threatened by foreign competitors. But the general pattern since Franklin D. Roosevelt in the 1930s has been that Republican and Democratic presidents alike have generally defended free trade, while the protectionist impulse has been confined mostly to Congress, notes Douglas Irwin, an economics professor at Dartmouth College and historian of American trade policy.
Trump’s willingness to impose tariffs on a panoramic list of US trading partners is unmatched since McKinley in the 1890s, says Alan Tonelson, a longtime manufacturing trade policy analyst and advocate for import restrictions. Irwin thinks Trump outmatches even McKinley: He believes Trump is pursuing the most confrontational trade policy since Jefferson imposed an (ultimately disastrous) 1807 embargo on all commerce with both England and Napoleon-era France in protest of their attacks on American shipping during their worldwide conflict. “There’s been no president in modern history who has used the tariff threat nearly as much as Donald Trump,” says Irwin.
Stanley Greenberg, a longtime Democratic pollster who has studied the party’s diminishing support among working-class white voters since the 1980s, says that Trump’s hardline approach on trade contributed to his 2016 breakthroughs against Hillary Clinton in battered blue-collar communities that had, in many cases, previously voted for Barack Obama during his two presidential victories.
“Hillary got hurt and Obama got hurt by not understanding these sentiments in the industrial Midwest,” Greenberg says. “And Trump used that to his advantage to win the election in 2016 and it was a fundamental part of his presidency in the first term, in which the association of him going after bad trade agreements and him championing tariffs” allowed him to present himself as a champion of “forgotten” working-class voters.
In his first term, Trump sharply veered from the preponderantly free trade outlook of his three immediate predecessors: Obama, George W. Bush and Bill Clinton. Trump renegotiated NAFTA, the free trade agreement that Clinton pushed through Congress; scrapped the pan-Asian free trade agreement that Obama had negotiated (but never submitted to Congress for fear of hurting Hillary Clinton in the 2016 election); and imposed tariffs primarily on steel and aluminum imports from many countries as well as a wide array of products from China.
But all that was barely an overture for Trump’s second term. To a far greater extent than in his first term, Trump has levied, withdrawn and reimposed tariffs; brandished threats; and launched investigations in a bewildering blur that has upended the rules of trade with dozens of countries. He has moved as aggressively against allies, such as Canada and the European Union, as against traditional trade adversaries such as China.
Before Trump, Holtz-Eakin notes, many political leaders believed “the politics were good” for protectionism, “but the foreign policy implications were bad.” As a result, “no Republican would go there,” he says. “But Trump didn’t care about the latter. So, we’ve (been able) to see the economics in isolation.” And the reaction has been very different than what Trump — and other trade hawks — expected.
Tariffs seemed more popular in theory than they are in practice
Since at least the 1970s, the dominant assumption in each party has been that trade issues divided the public along educational lines, with college-educated voters the most likely to favor expanding trade and working-class voters most receptive to a protectionist message of restricting imports to try to protect domestic manufacturing jobs.
That traditional divide persisted even as Trump returned to office. The Chicago Council on Global Affairs’ annual foreign policy polling, for instance, found that in 2025 nearly two-thirds of whites without a college degree preferred a trade policy that imposed restrictions on imports to protect jobs over an approach that minimized restrictions to lower prices. Whites with a college degree split evenly over which approach they preferred; notably, however, in a sharp departure from their white counterparts, a slight majority of nonwhites without a college degree preferred a trade policy that focused on costs. College-educated nonwhites were the most skeptical of all toward restrictions.
But as Trump has implemented his tariffs, they have proven less attractive for most Americans in practice than in theory. In Pew polling this January, 60% of Americans opposed his tariff increases; more than twice as many said it had affected their family negatively as positively. In a CNN/SSRS poll this April, four times as many Americans said the tariffs had hurt their personal finances as said they’d helped. Recent polls in Wisconsin and Ohio, two heavily working-class, manufacturing-oriented states, both found about 60% of residents opposed the tariffs. Polls released this month have found overwhelming opposition to Trump’s latest trade war against Canada, particularly in states along the border: In CNN surveys, about two-thirds or more of voters in both Michigan and Maine said the new Canadian tariffs were bad for their state.
