articles.title_zh: This Woman Who Lived in 14th-Century China May Have Had Her Nose Cut Off as Punishment for Theft or Adultery
articles.content_orig:
This Woman Who Lived in 14th-Century China May Have Had Her Nose Cut Off as Punishment for Theft or Adultery
Researchers found signs of healing on her 700-year-old skull, which suggests that she survived the painful sanction—and may even have gone on to wear a prosthesis
Cutting off a person’s nose without anesthesia was one of the “Five Punishments” that could be imposed in ancient China, along with decapitation, limb amputation, castration and facial tattooing. But although nasal amputations appear in historical texts, archaeologists had never found physical evidence of the painful penalty—until now.
Writing in a new paper published in the Journal of Archaeological Science: Reports, scientists describe the first skeletal evidence of facial mutilation as a form of punishment in ancient China.
In 2018, archaeologists were called in to survey an area of China’s Henan province ahead of the planned construction of a trade school. Their work revealed a burial ground containing 299 tombs.
Within the cemetery, they found the remains of a woman between ages 40 and 45 who’d been buried facedown, a position that suggests she may have experienced discrimination. Notably, the researchers didn’t find any other bodies in the cemetery buried this way. She was also buried alone, rather than inside a customary family or communal tomb.
“We believe this woman was a kind of castoff after death,” study co-author Qian Wang, a biological anthropologist at Texas A&M University, tells Live Science’s Kristina Killgrove.
Radiocarbon dating revealed that the woman lived between 1298 and 1404 C.E., during either the late Yuan or early Ming dynasty. The tomb’s design pointed to the Yuan dynasty.
Did you know? Punitive amputation
In 2024, Wang and his colleagues reported the discovery of two men who each had one leg punitively amputated. The remains were also found in China’s Henan province but date to around 550 B.C.E., during the Zhou dynasty.
An analysis of her remains suggests that she subsisted primarily on millet and consumed little animal protein, dietary patterns that might indicate her membership in a lower class.
When the researchers took a closer look at her skull, they made some unexpected discoveries. She had an enlarged piriform aperture, or nose opening, and substantial amounts of bone and tissue appeared to have been cut away from bottom to top.
These unusual features might have stemmed from a birth defect, an accident, a disease or even self-mutilation. However, given her burial position and probable low socioeconomic status, the researchers think the woman’s nose was more likely cut off.
They suspect she might have been punished for stealing horses or cattle. However, her nose may have been cut off for some other offense, such as adultery.
Whatever the reason, the woman appears to have received some sort of medical care after the amputation to “stop bleeding, prevent infection and reduce pain,” Wang tells Gizmodo’s Gayoung Lee. Her nasal bones show signs of healing, which means she survived the incident, though researchers think she may have had trouble breathing and moving her upper lip afterward.
And she may even have tried to resume a normal life. The formation of bone spurs around the nasal opening has led the team to believe that she may have worn a prosthetic nose.
However, her facedown interment seems to indicate that the people responsible for her burial sought to conceal her disfigurement. During the Yuan dynasty, such burials were sometimes associated with punishment, NewScientist’s Christa Lesté-Lasserre reports.
“I suspect she lived a difficult life, facing stigma and social challenges,” David Shaye, a surgeon at Harvard University who specializes in face, head and neck procedures and was not involved with the research, tells NewScientist. “Facial deformities can profoundly affect identity, social interaction and a person’s place within a community. In this sense, this archaeological finding connects very directly with challenges that people continue to face today.”
Though this may be the first documented example of nasal amputation, it likely won’t be the last. Now that researchers know what to look for, they can examine other ancient remains for similar injuries, Elizabeth Berger, a bioarchaeologist at the University of California, Riverside who was not involved with the research, tells Live Science.
“Hopefully more evidence can be found of who was subjected to this punishment, how it was carried out, and how it was medically managed afterwards, including the use of prosthetics,” she adds.

When Chinese President Xi Jinping arrives in Washington, he’s expected to get a rare greeting from President Donald Trump, who’ll be on the tarmac to welcome his counterpart’s plane instead of waiting for him to drive up to the White House

When Chinese President Xi Jinping arrives in Washington on Wednesday, he’s expected to get a rare greeting from President Donald Trump, who'll be on the tarmac to welcome his counterpart’s plane instead of waiting for him to drive up to the White House. Trump’s decision to greet Xi shows how far the U.S. president is going to honor China’s leader as he makes his first state visit in more than a decade.
Also, Trump’s AI-fueled vision for a drone port he intends to install atop the new White House ballroom includes missile-bearing unmanned aerial vehicles and gun-toting troops. But what hasn't been previously reported is the presence of a drone port a few hundred feet away, run by the U.S. Secret Service and not the military, which is already quietly operational.
Taiwan is watching closely as Xi and Trump meet and hopes US will keep up its arms sales
As China’s Xi Jinping arrives in Washington to meet with President Trump, Taiwan expressed confidence that U.S. arms sales to the island that Beijing claims as its own will continue — despite China’s pressure.
China has pressed Washington to halt the arms sales, most prominently during a summit in May between Trump and Xi in Beijing. After that meeting, the United States paused the sale of a record-breaking $14 billion package — and Trump described arms sales to Taiwan as a “very good negotiating chip” with China.
Still, the U.S. government and Congress have “repeatedly expressed support for Taiwan’s self-defense capabilities,” Taiwanese Defense Ministry spokesperson Maj. Gen. Chiao Fu-chun told reporters in the southern city of Tainan.
Trump says his ballroom will house a drone port. The Secret Service already has one next door
Trump’s AI-fueled vision for a drone port he intends to install atop the new White House ballroom includes missile-bearing unmanned aerial vehicles and gun-toting troops, ostensibly to protect the 18-acre complex and the nation’s capital.
A few hundred feet away, a drone port, run by the U.S. Secret Service and not the military, is already quietly operational. Equipped with cameras and sensors to scope out potential threats from a bird’s-eye view, the small UAVs stand on alert in four gray weatherproof boxes until deployed at officers’ commands.
The agency is using a model known as “drone as first responder,” deploying speedy unarmed drones from outdoor stations to serve as flying cameras. That model has been adopted by hundreds of police agencies across the U.S., often powered by AI software to help dodge obstacles or track targets.
The existence of the surveillance drones on a Treasury Department building adjacent to the White House complex has not been previously reported, and could undercut Trump’s legal claims that the ballroom construction is necessary “to protect the White House and surrounding region from aerial attacks.”
Xi is en route to Washington
Xi has departed Beijing on Wednesday afternoon local time for a state visit to the U.S., China’s official news agency Xinhua said. Accompanying him on the visit are Xi’s wife Peng Liyuan, China’s ruling Communist Party’s Politburo Standing Committee member Cai Qi and Foreign Minister Wang Yi, it said.
China’s Xi to kick off state visit to Washington with rare planeside welcome from Trump
When Chinese President Xi Jinping arrives in Washington on Wednesday, he’s expected to get a rare greeting from President Donald Trump, who will be on the tarmac to welcome his counterpart’s plane instead of waiting for him to drive up to the White House.
Trump’s decision to greet Xi at Joint Base Andrews shows how far the U.S. president is going to honor China’s leader as he makes his first state visit in more than a decade.
The White House hasn't released many details about Wednesday’s greeting, but Trump is expected to participate in an arrival ceremony at the base with Xi and his wife. The salutation will kick off a three-day visit that’s expected to be saturated with pomp, even by White House standards. The state visit, complete with a formal state dinner at the White House on Thursday, is supposed to reciprocate for the ceremonial grandeur that marked Trump’s May visit to China.
But it’s also a showy patina at a time when tensions between the two geopolitical rivals are high over trade, artificial intelligence, Trump’s war with Iran and China’s designs on Taiwan.

articles.title_orig: McDonald's will spend big on restaurant upgrades, training to drive growth
articles.title_zh: McDonald's will spend big on restaurant upgrades, training to drive growth
articles.content_orig:
McDonald's on Wednesday announced new financial targets for higher operating margins, a training program to improve food quality and plans to support franchisees financially as they invest in their restaurants.
It unveiled those efforts to improve its business ahead of an investor presentation that will kick off from the fast-food giant's Chicago headquarters at 9:30 a.m. ET on Wednesday.
In June, the company unveiled its newest growth strategy, McDonald's > NEXT. The pillars of the plan include a new restaurant design, better-tasting food and drinks, consumer-led innovation, and improved hospitality from employees. But until Wednesday, executives had offered few details about how they would implement the plan and how it may affect its financial results over the coming years.
The shifts come as McDonald's U.S. business tries to rebound from sluggish sales and as consumers hit by years of elevated inflation visit restaurants less often.
Programming note: McDonald's CEO Chris Kempczinski will speak to CNBC's "Squawk on the Street" at 10 a.m. ET. Watch live on CNBC or CNBC+.
A key part of the strategy is restaurant remodels, which McDonald's mandates roughly every decade for franchisees. But the chain will also unveil what it calls Restaurant > NEXT, which includes improvements to equipment, technology and operations. It also will feature "ArchIQ," an artificial intelligence-powered operating system for restaurants.
All of those upgrades will require steep investment from franchisees. But McDonald's is also planning to provide financial support, through rent relief and actual capital. Through 2036, McDonald's plans to spend as much as $8.5 billion to accelerate franchisees' investment in the restaurant improvement plan.
About $5 billion of that support will happen through 2030. McDonald's is projecting about $1.5 billion to $2 billion in capital spending from 2027 through 2030 to accelerate NEXT, in addition to about $3 billion every year on typical capital expenditures. (In 2025, McDonald's reported $3.4 billion in capital expenditures.)
Franchisees may protest the franchisor's expectations for their own investment in the restaurants, on top of standard cosmetic remodels. Beef and labor costs are already weighing on their profits.
But executives think that the upgrades will pay off for their locations. McDonald's projects that efficiency improvements will result in an increase of roughly $100,000 in annual cash flow for the average U.S. restaurant, and the initiative will take about four years to return franchisees' investment.
While McDonald's plans to spend more to fuel restaurant improvements, the company said it aims to cut costs elsewhere, although it did not offer specifics. By 2030, McDonald's is targeting an operating margin in the low-to-mid 50% range. In 2025, the company reported operating margins of 46.1%, according to company filings.
Some of that margin expansion will come from its general and administrative spending. By 2030, McDonald's is projecting that about 1.9% of its systemwide sales will go toward G&A. For comparison, the company is currently forecasting that 2.2% of its systemwide sales will be spent on G&A in 2026.
McDonald's also has an eye on growing its sales globally. Some of that will come from new locations. Next year, the company expects restaurant openings will make up about 2.5% of its systemwide sales growth.
The company's accelerated expansion will slow in the following years. By 2030, McDonald's anticipates new restaurants will account for only about 2% of growth to systemwide sales.
In recent years, the burger chain has leaned into menu items other than its core beef offerings to drive sales, namely chicken and beverages. By 2030, McDonald's wants to grow its global market share in those two categories by about 1.5 percentage points each.
Still, McDonald's isn't abandoning burgers. The company wants to hold onto its leadership in beef, too.
To do so, it plans on implementing "Make It Golden," a multiyear employee training program to ensure consistency, improved quality and better customer service. The program will begin rolling out on Oct. 5, the 124th birthday of Ray Kroc, who turned the burger restaurant into a global giant.

articles.title_orig: Capitol agenda: Republicans riddled by stay-or-go dilemma
articles.title_zh: Capitol agenda: Republicans riddled by stay-or-go dilemma
articles.content_orig:
Republicans have long ridiculed Jimmy Carter as a feckless figure who did little to help a limping economy and was outsmarted by foreign adversaries like Iran. President Donald Trump once used the occasion of Carter’s 100th birthday, in October 2024, to declare him a success — at least compared with Joe Biden.
Now, with few options at their disposal to tackle the record-high diesel prices battering farmers and truck drivers, and with just six weeks to go until the midterms, growing pockets of the Republican Party are reaching into the Carter playbook.
In the past three days, the concept of a diesel export ban caught fire among Republican lawmakers. Sen. Chuck Grassley of Iowa spearheaded the GOP jailbreak when he endorsed the proposal on Saturday, saying in an X post that “high diesel prices ARE KILLING FARMERS INCOME.”
Now a stampede of Iowa Republicans is rushing to back the proposal, as diesel scaled to a record high of $6.53 per gallon nationwide. It’s more than double the price from a year ago, thanks in large part to the Iran war and, to a lesser extent, the war in Ukraine. Republicans are demanding immediate action.
“Iowa farmers are filling combines this week at the highest diesel price this state has ever seen, while oil companies ship record amounts of American diesel overseas,” Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks said, calling companies to “sell American diesel to Americans first.” The three-term congresswoman’s re-election race has been rated as a toss-up by Inside Elections, a nonpartisan publication.
Rep. Ashley Hinson, who is campaigning to replace retiring Sen. Joni Ernst as Iowa’s next senator, joined the pack as well. Other House Republicans also introduced legislation last week to implement a temporary diesel export ban through January 2027 just before they skipped town until after the Nov. 3 midterms.
For now, there’s little to indicate that the White House is seriously considering a diesel export ban. On Tuesday, Trump said he had “called for it within my people,” and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the administration was studying its overall feasibility.
Diesel prices have shot up about 70% since the Trump administration and Israel launched their war with Iran in late February. Different from gasoline, diesel fuel powers the large trucks and heavy freight vehicles carrying food, furniture, clothing and energy products to their destinations. It’s also critical in operating farm and construction equipment, as well as the composition of home heating oil. Diesel is the concealed lifeblood of the U.S. economy, and Republicans are panicking that its price is about to spiral out of control.
The fact that Republicans from ruby-red states are clamoring for government intervention underscores the dwindling levers they have left to pull in their campaigns to keep control of the House and Senate. Polls have shown Republicans are struggling to persuade voters to give them another chance to quell rising prices, with inflation topping their list of concerns. That’s hard to pull off when Trump has dismissed affordability as a “fake” Democratic-manufactured crisis as recently as the GOP midterm convention.
And so Republicans are falling back on a Carter-era idea that only deepened rock bottom for farmers.

articles.title_orig: China is investigating DeepSeek and Moonshot over data that flowed to Anthropic
articles.title_zh: China is investigating DeepSeek and Moonshot over data that flowed to Anthropic
articles.content_orig:
China's Cyberspace Administration is investigating DeepSeek and Moonshot AI over user data that may have reached Anthropic's servers without customers' knowledge, according to The Information. Officials have visited both firms to question executives and staff, and the investigation is ongoing with no determination on penalties yet made.
The trigger was a 154-page threat intelligence report Anthropic published on Sept. 10, in which the company accused seven China-based AI labs of routing customer requests through Claude to harvest its outputs for model training — a practice Anthropic calls illicit distillation. The seven companies named were Alibaba, Moonshot AI, DeepSeek, Zhipu, MiniMax, Xiaomi, and SenseTime. Once the report was out, the Cyberspace Administration called in representatives from all seven named companies before ultimately concentrating on DeepSeek and Moonshot, according to The Information.
Beijing's concern runs in the opposite direction from Anthropic's. Anthropic's grievance is that Chinese labs extracted its model's capabilities. The regulator's concern is what traveled the other way: Chinese users' data landing on an American company's servers without those users' knowledge, potentially violating Chinese data security laws.
Anthropic's report provided specific examples involving both companies. In one case, a user whom Anthropic identified as affiliated with the People's Liberation Army asked Kimi, Moonshot's chatbot, to examine surveillance video of a single individual captured across hundreds of police cameras in Chengdu, among them cameras positioned outside PLA facilities and defense-linked institutes. According to the report, Moonshot then passed both the request and the footage along to Claude, all without the user's awareness. In another case, DeepSeek relayed requests from engineers building a police surveillance case management system, exposing live credentials tied to a Russian government database.
According to Anthropic, Moonshot sent over 23 million exchanges through Claude in the May-to-July window, while DeepSeek's operation generated more than 12.1 million exchanges in just a 14-day stretch during July. In both cases, the report found, users had no idea their queries were being handled by Anthropic's system.
The timing carries complications for both companies. DeepSeek is scheduled to brief the United Nations Security Council this week on AI risks during the General Assembly, according to The Next Web. Moonshot faces a different problem: the company confidentially filed for a Hong Kong IPO targeting $3 billion, and an open regulatory investigation would require disclosure in any prospectus.
The probe also arrives as President Xi Jinping prepares to visit Washington later this week, where AI is expected to feature in discussions with President Donald Trump, including a proposed mechanism for notifying each other about AI incidents with national security implications, according to The Information.
The combined distillation activity across all seven companies totaled roughly 190 million exchanges, with Alibaba accounting for more than 151 million — far more than any other named company. Despite that scale, Alibaba is not currently the subject of the CAC inquiry. The regulator has not set a timetable or indicated whether it will penalize either DeepSeek or Moonshot.

Iran War Updates: U.S. and Iran hold first talks since June after Trump threatens regime with annihilation
What to know about the Iran war today:
- Iranian state media say the country's president will address the United Nations General Assembly Wednesday, after President Trump said the first talks between U.S. and Iranian envoys in months went well the previous day.
- The Iran-backed Houthi rebels threatened Wednesday to attack U.S. interests in the Middle East and to "close Bab el-Mandeb completely to American ships" if Washington joins Saudi-led military operations against the group in Yemen.
- Mr. Trump told the General Assembly Tuesday that he had a "big decision to make" on whether to seek a deal to end the nearly 7-month war, or to "annihilate" Iran and drive it "into hell with no chance of survival."
Countries suspend Iranian airline flights as U.S. sanctions take effect
Several countries began suspending flights operated by Iranian airlines to their airports on Wednesday as new U.S. sanctions targeting the country's aviation sector took effect.
The Trump administration announced earlier this month that Iran's entire air transport sector would be subject to sanctions. U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warned that Iranian airlines would face difficulties operating globally from Sept. 23.
Georgia has banned flights operated by Iranian carriers from the country, while Iran's Mahan Air suspended flights to Turkey at Ankara's request.
Azerbaijan has also suspended Iranian flights, citing the new U.S. sanctions.
Iraq ordered the suspension of Iranian flights to Baghdad International Airport from Wednesday, according to the Reuters news agency. Iraqi authorities were, however, considering redirecting the flights to the central city of Najaf, an important Shiite Muslim pilgrimage destination.
"The decision does not mean a complete suspension of flights to Iraq, and that flights to other airports, including Najaf airport, will continue to operate as usual for all Iranian airlines," Iraqi Civil Aviation Organization spokesman Majid Akhavan said in remarks to Iranian media.
Iran's Civil Aviation Organization said flights from Tehran to Baghdad and Muscat, Oman, were canceled from Wednesday, while other remaining international flights, including those to Istanbul, would continue according to schedule.
It added that Iranian passengers were not being allowed to enter Oman's airport, with consultations underway on the issue.
Houthis threaten to target U.S. interests in Mideast if Washington intervenes in Yemen's civil war
The Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen will attack U.S. interests in the Middle East if Washington intervenes in the conflict in support of Saudi Arabia, including by attempting to thwart Houthi efforts to blockade Saudi shipping through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a military adviser for the group told the AFP news agency Wednesday.
"If America dares to intervene militarily with its fleets or tries to take control of Bab el-Mandeb, it is a red line for them and anyone else … we will fight over it," Houthi military adviser Abed Mohammed al-Thawr told the AFP.
The Houthis have dislodged Saudi-backed government forces from Yemen's Red Sea coast in recent weeks in fighting that has left hundreds dead. Houthi drones and missiles have also targeted Saudi sites, including the capital Riyadh, for the first time in years.
Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman requested help from President Trump in fighting the Houthis earlier in September, two sources familiar with the matter told CBS News. Yemen's government also made the request, a well-placed source told AFP.
The Houthis say Saudi Arabia has conducted hundreds of strikes in Yemen since fighting resumed in July, effectively ending a four-year truce.
"If America gambles on supporting Saudi Arabia with airstrikes or air support ... We will consider any American interests around us to be targets and we will not exclude anything," Thawr told AFP, adding that the group would "close Bab el-Mandeb completely to American ships."
Thawr denied receiving directives from Iran, but said they were "one alliance and one body."
"Iran is a friendly, allied, and brotherly country to us, but it does not direct us. We are independent in our decisions and in our sovereignty," he said.
Iran calls Trump's U.N. speech "a sign of desperation"
Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei has said that President Trump's remarks to the U.N. were "a sign of desperation."
Speaking to state news agency IRNA, Baqaei also confirmed the talks held between U.S. and Iranian envoys on Tuesday took place via Qatari mediators.
"The Iranian delegation conveyed its views and its conditions very explicitly and clearly to the American side through the mediators," he said.
Addressing Mr. Trump's remarks about his pending "big decision" on whether to make a deal with, or "annihilate" the Iranian regime, Baqaei said: "The impression among diplomats and delegations from many countries here was that these remarks did not stem from strength, but from desperation … Threatening a country with military attack is an admission of the nature of the current U.S. ruling establishment."
U.S. and Iranian negotiators "successfully completed" indirect talks in NYC, Witkoff says
U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff said American and Iranian negotiators "engaged in lengthy talks" on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly.
In a post on X late Tuesday, Witkoff said the two sides spoke through mediators over the course of the day. He did not describe the substance of the talks, but said they "successfully completed a round of discussions that we hope will prove constructive and promising."
President Trump told reporters earlier Tuesday that Witkoff and U.S. envoy Jared Kushner had a "very good meeting," and the two sides "have another one scheduled in the very near future."
Trump meets with Gulf leaders on sidelines of U.N. General Assembly
President Trump joined a meeting of the Gulf Cooperation Council on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly, where the president said there's a "lot of momentum" for Iran to make a deal. Countries represented in the meeting included Jordan, Saudi Arabia, Qatar and Turkey.
"I like these people," the president said of the leaders around him.
The president said Iran's economy is in bad shape, and he hopes they do something good for their people.
"I don't think about the election at all when I think about ending the nuclear threat from Iran. I just think about ending the nuclear threat from Iran," he said.
U.S. delegation, including Kushner and Witkoff, met with Iranian officials, Trump says
President Trump said U.S. and Iranian officials met on Tuesday, shortly after threatening in his address to the U.N. General Assembly that he may "annihilate" the Islamic Republic if a deal isn't reached soon to end the nearly seven-month war.
Mr. Trump told reporters the meeting happened, and ended "about an hour ago," but offered few details about the talks.
"It was a very good meeting," Mr. Trump said. "They have another one scheduled in the very near future."
The meeting lasted about three hours, Mr. Trump said, and his son-in-law, Jared Kushner, and special envoy Steve Witkoff were part of it.
Witkoff echoed that the meeting went well, saying "I feel very good right now," but provided no further details.
Iran and U.S. held peace talks Tuesday, Trump says
The U.S. and Iran held talks Tuesday while both countries are at the U.N. for this week's General Assembly, President Trump said. He also said he believes the U.S. will come to an agreement with Iran, though he did not specify when.
"I think that a settlement is going to be reached," Mr. Trump said during a bilateral meeting with U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham. "They want to talk to us. They have been talking to us. Even today, they've been talking to us, and the relationship is developing, let's say."

Trump to meet with China's Xi as Congress mulls bill banning artificial superintelligence
Hello and welcome to the US politics live blog.
Donald Trump will meet with the Chinese president Xi Jinping later today, ahead of a three-day visit that will undoubtedly see artificial intelligence (AI) high on the agenda.
António Guterres, the UN secretary general, has called on the two countries to establish a dialogue on AI similar to the communication between the US and the Soviet Union during the cold war.
“Governments with the greatest AI capabilities have the greatest responsibilities to humanity, to establish channels for dialogue, transparency, trust and cooperation,” Guterres said.
Tech executives including Jeff Bezos of Amazon, Sundar Pichai of Alphabet, Sam Altman of OpenAI, Tim Cook of Apple, Elon Musk of Tesla, Mark Zuckerberg of Meta and Jensen Huang of Nvidia will reportedly attend a state dinner at the White House on Thursday evening.
It comes as two leading progressive US lawmakers, senator Bernie Sanders and representative Greg Casar, were due to unveil legislation later today that would ban artificial superintelligence and create a federal agency to oversee advanced AI.
The bill, provided first to the Associated Press, would also pause advanced AI development until guidelines are implemented while creating the Department of Artificial Intelligence. Multiple employees at leading AI companies are endorsing the bill.
“It doesn’t take a genius to say, ‘slow it down,’” Sanders said in an interview with AP. “Do we really want to develop a super intelligence that when it becomes smarter than human beings could act independently of human control? I don’t think we do.”
Congress has so far done little to rein in the AI industry even as some of its most prominent leaders warn about potentially catastrophic risks.
Xi departed Beijing on Wednesday, state media said, heading to Joint Base Andrews, Maryland, where he will be met by Trump on the tarmac.
“President Xi Jinping left Beijing by special plane for a state visit to the United States” accompanied by his wife Peng Liyuan, his right-hand man Cai Qi, and foreign minister Wang Yi, among others, state broadcaster CCTV said.
Speaking at the UN general assembly, Donald Trump re-issued his threat to “annihilate” Iran and “drive them into Hell” if the regime didn’t capitulate and make a deal.” He also said he was “working closely with the leaders of Russia and Ukraine” to end the disastrous war, defended his administration’s actions in Latin America – including the midnight raid to arrest former Venezuelan president Nicólas Maduro, defended his drone strikes on boats in the Caribbean and the Pacific, accused Mexico of being effectively controlled by the cartels, and said it was “unacceptable” for the US to share a border with a nation under such conditions, pointed to regime change in Cuba and said he would reject any calls for a “globalist scheme” to control artificial intelligence.
Shortly after his UN address, Trump signed a Greenland deal, which Greenland’s prime minister Jens-Frederick Nielsen said “underlines the importance of the Nato alliance.” In tricky, carefully worded paragraphs, she said the agreement “recognises the US defining historical and ongoing contributions to the security and defence of Greenland,” but it also “respects the sovereignty and the territorial integrity of the Kingdom of Denmark, as well as Greenland’s right to self-determination.”
Trump told a CNN reporter at the UN general assembly on Tuesday that he was “surprised” the outlet was covering him, saying it ‘shouldn’t be here’ after he banned the network alongside Politico and MS Now from the White House on Friday.
At a joint press conference on Tuesday, vice-president JD Vance and Mehmet Oz, administrator of the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, announced that the federal government was removing 760,000 enrollees from Affordable Care Act insurance marketplaces.
The Trump administration is refusing to work with the newly appointed deputy head of the United Nations refugee agency, Reuters reported.
Tressa Rae Finerty, an American who took up the role of deputy high commissioner at UNHCR earlier this month, has taken leave as she seeks a waiver from the US government that would allow her to carry out aspects of her duties, according to seven diplomatic sources.
Her treatment by Washington, which previously considered cutting ties with the agency, is seen by several of the diplomats as a retaliatory response after UNHCR opted against Washington’s preferred candidate, Simon Hankinson.
A State Department spokesperson said it could not comment on pending legal issues. “We work with and through UNHCR when doing so advances US foreign policy interests,” the spokesperson said.

Hurricane Polo, an extremely powerful Category 4 storm, swirls off Mexico's Pacific coast. See its path.
Hurricane Polo, an extremely powerful Category 4 storm, continued to swirl off Mexico's southwestern coast early Wednesday but was only expected to skirt the Pacific shoreline over the next few days, not make landfall, as it continues along its path.
The U.S. National Hurricane Center said Polo's maximum sustained winds — which had rapidly intensified Tuesday, reaching as high as a 180 mph — decreased somewhat to 150 mph, not far beneath the 157 mph threshold which would make it a Category 5, the strongest on the hurricane scale.
The storm is expected to fluctuate in intensity over the next few days, forecasters said, but remain a "very powerful major hurricane."
Maps show Hurricane Polo's path
As of early Wednesday, Polo was located about 165 miles off the coast of Zihuatanejo, a coastal resort city in the Mexican state of Guerrero. Polo's outer rain bands were starting to reach the coast, the hurricane center said.
It hurled hurricane-force winds outward up to 40 miles from its center and tropical storm-force winds some 105 miles out, but was roughly stationary, crawling northward at 2 mph.
Polo was forecast to bring tropical storm conditions to parts of the coastline starting Wednesday. In some areas, heavy rainfall "may produce life-threatening flooding and mudslides, especially in areas of steep terrain," the hurricane center warned.
The storm remains far south of Mexico's Baja California peninsula, but the longer-term forecast indicates it could turn in that direction early next week.
The Mexican government issued a tropical storm warning for a stretch of the Mexican coast from Tecpan de Galeana, in Guerrero, to Punta San Telmo, in Michoacán. A tropical storm watch was in effect from Punta San Telmo to Playa Perula, in the state of Jalisco. Tropical storm warnings are issued when forecasts indicate tropical storm conditions will develop in a particular area, while tropical storm watches are issued when those conditions are possible, but not imminent.
In this case, the hurricane center said people under a tropical storm warning should expect those conditions to take shape on Wednesday. For those in the watch area, such conditions could develop by Thursday.
Parts of Guerrero and Michoacán may receive between 3 and 6 inches of rainfall as Polo barrels past, with up to 8 inches possible in certain spots, through Thursday. Between 2 and 4 inches of rain could also fall in coastal parts of the states of Oaxaca, Colima and Jalisco through Thursday, forecasters said.
Along with rain, Polo was also expected to cause life-threatening surf conditions, including rip currents, along the southwestern Mexican coast. The surf conditions could also contribute to flooding.
Polo is the second-strongest hurricane on record in terms of its central pressure in the Eastern Pacific (behind Patricia in 2015) and tied for third-strongest in terms of wind speed (along with Rick in 2009).
Unusually strong El Niño conditions this year have been amping up tropical cyclone activity in the Pacific, with warmer waters, moist air and less wind shear enabling storm formation.

articles.title_zh: US fixed 30-year mortgage rate jumps to 7.12%, MBA says
articles.content_orig:
Sept 23 (Reuters) - The rate on the most popular US home loan rose last week to its highest in more than two years, after the Federal Reserve lifted short-term interest rates to combat inflation, and rising oil prices drove up Treasury yields that underpin residential borrowing costs.
The average 30-year fixed-rate mortgage jumped 15 basis points to 7.12% in the week ended September 18, the Mortgage Bankers Association said on Wednesday. It was last higher in May 2024.
Mortgage rates have risen more than a full percentage point since joint US-Israeli strikes against Iran began pushing up the global price of oil in late February, putting the squeeze on prospective homebuyers and a chill into the US housing market.
Mortgage rates track US Treasury yields, which are sensitive to oil prices and the threat they pose to inflation, which has been running above the Fed's 2% goal for 5-1/2 years.
Last week the Fed increased its policy rate by a quarter of a percentage point to the 3.75%-4.00% range to put inflation on a "timelier" path to 2%, and nearly all Fed policymakers projected at least one more rate increase by the end of this year. Traders are also betting on further Fed rate hikes.
The rise in mortgage rates last week led to a decline in refinancing and home purchase applications, the MBA said, and drove more borrowers into adjustable-rate mortgages, which offer lower upfront borrowing costs than fixed-rate mortgages and reset after a number of years to whatever the going rate is at the time. ARMs accounted for 9.8% of mortgage applications last week, the MBA said.

Mortgage rates soared to the highest level since 2024 last week, causing loan demand to fall back again and more borrowers to opt for riskier loans. Total application volume decreased 1.5% from the previous week, according to the Mortgage Bankers Association's seasonally adjusted index.
The average contract interest rate for 30-year fixed-rate mortgages with conforming loan balances, $832,750 or less, increased to 7.12% from 6.97%, with points rising to 0.73 from 0.72, including the origination fee, for loans with a 20% down payment.
Applications to refinance a home loan dropped 3% for the week and were 62% lower than the same week one year ago. That was the lowest level since February 2025. The 30-year fixed loan was 78 basis points, or more than three-quarters of a percentage point lower, at the same time last year.
Applications for a mortgage to purchase a home fell 1% for the week and were 11% lower year over year. The fall housing market, usually the second busiest compared with spring, is now underway, but real estate agents are already noting a sharp pullback due to higher rates. Buyers and current homeowners are also searching for savings anywhere they can find them, even in riskier, adjustable-rate loans.
"With fixed rates much higher, more borrowers opted for ARMs, with the ARM share reaching 9.8%, as rates for 5/1 ARMs were more than a percentage point lower than those for fixed rate loans," said Mike Fratantoni, senior vice president and chief economist at the MBA.
The ARM share of applications the week before last was just 8.4%. During the first years of the pandemic, when rates were hitting multiple record lows, the ARM share was barely 3%. ARMs can carry a fixed rate for up to 10 years but will adjust either higher or lower depending on where the market is when that term is up.
Mortgage rates moved slightly lower to start this week, according to a separate survey from Mortgage News Daily, as the price of oil fell and bond yields moved lower as a result.

Oil prices edged higher on Wednesday after President Trump floated a diesel export ban the previous day, with industry analysts warning that such a measure could backfire.
Brent crude futures (BZ=F) for November delivery hovered near $100 per barrel while WTI (CL=F)) futures hovered around $90 a barrel.
Trump said Tuesday that he would support a ban on exports of diesel fuel.
"I've said let's not send out the diesel," the president said on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly. "We make a lot of diesel. It could have a little bit of an effect on regular automobile gasoline because when you do that, you know, it's a sort of a flow. It's a balance."
The national average price of diesel fuel has surged to an all-time record of $6.52 per gallon, according to AAA,
Analysts see an export ban as a further strain on global energy prices.
"We believe any possible US diesel export restriction could significantly tighten global supply further and benefit Asian refiners," wrote Citi analysts on Wednesday.
Wall Street argues that US refineries wouldn't be able to process all the trapped domestic fuel, ultimately reducing total fuel supplies. While Gulf states may initially see localized relief, other areas of the country that depend on fuel imports would see a spike in pump prices.
"This immediately causes those prices to rise, and will boomerang back on portions of the country that rely on imports, namely the East Coast and to a lesser extent the West Coast," said Garrett Golding, assistant VP for energy programs at the Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas on X regarding a diesel export ban.
Lower production rates overall could also mean "even higher gasoline prices as well," said Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis for GasBuddy on X on Wednesday.

articles.content_orig:
China's Great Green Wall pushes back Gobi sands, and the scale is hard to grasp
A sweeping video gave viewers a striking look at one of the world's most ambitious restoration efforts. China's Great Green Wall is an ambitious program to hold back desert sands in Inner Mongolia.
Shared by the South China Morning Post (@scmp.news), the clip shows a long strip of greenery meeting the edge of the Gobi, with the vegetation holding the sand at bay.
"China's Great Green Wall stands against the spread of desert sands," the caption stated.
Desertification can swallow productive land, worsen dust storms, strain water resources, and make life harder for people living near vulnerable drylands.
"The goal is to prevent the spread of desertification from affecting the country's interior," Zhao Zhong, founder of Green Camel Bell, told SCMP. "So far the most visible part of this effort is large-scale afforestation."
When restoration succeeds at scale, the benefits can be significant. Efforts can protect homes, roads, farms, and local economies from mounting land loss.
"This is what long-term environmental restoration looks like," a commenter wrote. "Seeing the greenery return is remarkable. Imagine what another few decades of careful restoration could accomplish."
China's Great Green Wall is a long-term effort to slow the advance of desert landscapes by planting trees and other vegetation across vulnerable northern regions.
SCMP said the program used the "straw checkerboards" planting technique to help nearby greenery by kickstarting an irrigation system. It also stabilizes sand dunes against strong winds.
In practical terms, such projects are meant to anchor soil, reduce erosion, and create buffers that limit how easily sand moves into settled or cultivated areas.
When land degradation spreads, it can lower agricultural productivity, reduce air quality, and stress infrastructure with blowing sand and dust. Reversing those trends can support public health, food security, and economic stability.
"It has replaced desertification with a slowly expanding wall of green in communities across half of China," SCMP noted in the video.
Desert control depends on investment, maintenance, and land management over decades.
SCMP reported that the initiative has reduced desert spread by nearly 400 miles a year since 2000 and created forests spanning almost 200,000 square miles.
If vegetation reduces erosion and buffers settlements from sand encroachment, people living nearby may benefit from cleaner air, more stable land, and stronger local resilience. In the video, locals touted the progress of the initiative.
Zhu Jiaojun of the Chinese Academy of Science warned that consolidating the gains of the initiative might be the real test.
"Given such high levels of investment and such massive input, once it stops, can what we achieved be sustained?" he said.
SCMP concluded by saying local green groups are educating new farmers and herders on the importance of preventing desertification.
China is engaging in a number of large-scale efforts to fight desertification in the country.
• Officials completed a shelterbelt 46 years in the making around the Taklimakan Desert.
• Authorities used a revolutionary strategy to turn barren land into wetlands.
• Along the Great Wall of China, biocrusts shield weak points from further erosion.

The continuing exchange of aerial attacks, even as front-line positions remain largely unchanged. Russia invaded Ukraine more than 4½ years ago. Still, Trump said Tuesday, "I think we're going to make a deal" to quell the fighting. "We talked about it a lot, including with President Putin," Trump said of a possible agreement, meaning Russian leader Vladmir Putin. "And I think something's going to happen." Putin is not scheduled to attend the annual U.N. General Assembly meeting this year. He also noted that Ukraine has continued to push the U.S. for more Patriot air defense systems in its efforts to defend itself, but has yet to get clear answers. "They are positive to help us, but I didn't get the very concrete answer," Zelenskyy said. Defense experts say the U.S. has been experiencing a global shortage of Patriot interceptors because many have been expended to defend against Iranian attacks on U.S. and allied bases in Middle East. Zelenskyy was also asked about the risk of offensive attacks by drones, missiles or land operations ordered by Moscow that could be high against other countries that border Russia or Belarus. He said such neighboring countries should "respond — always respond" to defend themselves. "If you don't respond," he added, "Russians, they will go further." Zelenskyy says Ukraine may end strikes if Russia makes concessions Kyiv began targeting Russian refineries after Moscow repeatedly attacked Ukraine's power grid. Zelenskyy says his country could halt them should Russia end its attacks on energy infrastructure. The war, which Western officials say has killed more than 500,000 Russian troops, has had global repercussions. Western analysts estimate that Ukraine has recorded more than 500,000 military casualties, including up to 140,000 deaths. Zelenskyy also wants help to ensure the flow of Ukrainian grain and other farm products to world markets through the Black Sea. Russian attacks on cargo vessels have severely disrupted Kyiv's exports, hurting its economy and threatening global supplies. Russia and Ukraine have in recent years accounted for around 30% of the world's wheat exports and 12% of corn exports, most of it shipped through the Black Sea. But last month, attacks slashed both countries' agricultural exports by two-thirds, Thomas de Waal of the Brussels-based think tank Carnegie Europe said in a report Tuesday. articles.title_orig: Polo off Mexican coast is among ‘the strongest storms ever’ as Odalys becomes a hurricane
articles.title_zh: Polo off Mexican coast is among ‘the strongest storms ever’ as Odalys becomes a hurricane
articles.content_orig:
A tropical storm off the south-west coast of Mexico has intensified into a category 5 monster in fewer than 24 hours, fueled by stronger than usual El Niño weather patterns in the Pacific Ocean.
Hurricane Polo was sending out maximum sustained winds of 165mph (266km/h) on Tuesday as its center churned about 215 miles (346km) south of the coastal city of Zihuatanejo, in Guerrero state.
On Monday, Polo was only a tropical storm with winds below 74mph (120km/h). Its rapid and sudden growth is testament to the dominance of this year’s so-called super El Niño, which set a record on Monday as the most extreme on record, and has amplified a number of extreme weather events globally.
Forecasters at the National Hurricane Center in Miami said Mexico was likely to avoid a direct hit, but warned that further intensification was likely, and that life-threatening flooding and mudslides were possible inland, along with dangerous surf and rip current conditions.
El Niño occurs when extended ocean temperatures in the eastern and central Pacific, and near the equator, rise above their historical average.
Meteorologists say the phenomenon increases disruptive winds and curtails other conditions favorable to storm development in the Atlantic basin, which remains quiet with less than three months to go in this year’s hurricane season.
Conversely, it promotes increased activity in the Pacific, where the 2026 El Niño remains one of the strongest on record.
“The water temperatures in two separate areas, the north-central Pacific and off the Mexican coast, are running well above average,” Paul Pastelok, AccuWeather’s lead long-range meteorologist, said in the online weather service’s fall hurricane outlook last month.
“We are seeing a strong impact in both the Atlantic and Pacific basins, with extreme wind shear limiting Atlantic storm development, while the Pacific remains quite active, as we expected back in the spring.”
Hurricane Polo’s single-day intensification also fits into the assessment of University of Miami senior research associate Brian McNoldy on his tropical Atlantic blog that El Niño, which he said was only “moderate” towards the beginning of September, was “forecast to become very strong, likely the strongest on record, by later this fall and into winter”.
Polo is the 18th named storm, and seventh hurricane, of the 2026 Pacific season, which runs from 15 May until 30 November.
By contrast, the Atlantic basin, which has a six-month season from June until November, has seen only six named tropical storms and no hurricanes so far.
It is the first time in 112 years that no Atlantic hurricanes have formed by 21 September, and 2026 could join 1907 and 1914 as the only years without one being recorded.

China's President Xi Jinping is set to arrive on U.S. soil later Wednesday for what is expected to be a tense showdown between President Donald Trump and the communist leader.
A red carpet rollout is planned for when Xi and his wife, Peng Liyuan, arrive at Joint Base Andrews on Wednesday evening, replete with an arrival ceremony for the man who has found himself at odds with Trump on issues ranging from artificial intelligence and intellectual property theft, trade practices, rare-earth minerals to the communist country's support for Iran during America's military conflict there. Xi hasn't visited the nation's capital in more than a decade.
AI will be a major topic of discussion during the two-day summit, which officially begins Thursday morning and ends Friday evening, according to a senior administration official. Thursday will begin with a prestigious State Arrival Ceremony, including 479 military personnel from all branches on the South Lawn, State Floor and Rose Garden of the White House.

According to the official, a wide-ranging deal on possible tariff reductions on non-strategic goods is an expected topic of discussion, who also said the nation's leaders will discuss rare-earth exports and possible export controls. Trump is also expected to press China to do more to curb fentanyl precursor chemical exports.
Trump is also likely to press for the release of an American who has been wrongfully detained in China, Gulshan Abbas, who has languished in a Chinese prison for eight years. The country accused her of "participating in a terrorist organization" after her sister spoke out about China's genocide of Uyghurs, according to Forbes. House Speaker Mike Johnson and other Republicans have expressed confidence that Trump will push for her release.

First lady Melania Trump is expected to accompany Peng to the Smithsonian National Museum of Asian Art, "to explore works spanning centuries of artistic achievement and Sino-American cultural exchange."
The day will end with an elaborate state dinner with high-profile guests, including many from the tech world.
Those guests will include Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, SpaceX founder and former Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) head Elon Musk, Google CEO Sundar Pichai, Dell Technologies CEO Michael Dell, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Citigroup CEO Jane Fraser and Apple Board of Directors Chairman Tim Cook.
Trump boasted about American AI supremacy over China during an address to the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) in New York Tuesday, using his newly-minted term for the technology, "superintelligence."

"Every major new technology brings challenges, and superintelligence is no exception," said Trump. "Whoever wins superintelligence wins. That's the group that wins. And we're leading now over China by a lot and everyone else. And we're going to keep it that way."
Trump traveled to Beijing in May where he met with Xi, and the two sides agreed to a "constructive" trade truce, pausing a tit-for-tat tariff battle, but only for non-strategic goods. For Quincy's Chinese community, the American dream lives on, with caveats
When Ziqiang Yuan moved to the U.S. in 1999, democracy was the last thing on her mind. Political speech was suppressed under socialist rule in her native China, and her aversion to politics stayed with her when she emigrated.
“We have a saying in China, ‘不谈政治.’ That means, ‘don't talk about politics,’ ” Yuan said. “You can get in trouble.”
Yuan, 55, goes by Susan now. She left Wuhan for the U.S. to pursue a post-doc in biomedical research, a field that then offered few opportunities in China while demand here was high. She even landed a scholarship.
But when her landlady brought Yuan to a local municipal meeting, eager to show the young grad student what American democracy looked like, something changed in Yuan. She was impressed that ordinary people were even aware of government gatherings, let alone that they could attend.
“That city council meeting really opened my eyes,” Yuan said. “You can have a chance to speak — directly speak — to those officials.”
Decades later, that first brush with local government would lead Yuan to try her chances at politics, a pathway she couldn’t have imagined had she stayed in China.
Yuan is among 175,000 people of Chinese descent who call Massachusetts home, including one in six Quincy residents. For most of U.S. history, Chinese immigrants have journeyed here in hopes of a better life. Their aspirations have varied decade to decade, and person to person. Indeed, ask people in Quincy about the American dream and the answers are as varied as the food options along Hancock and Beale streets.
Interviews with Chinese immigrants spanning multiple generations suggest the allure of the U.S. is being put to the test, amid a torrent of immigration restrictions under President Trump and the emergence of China as the world’s second-largest economy. But for many, the core draw of America remains strong, whether that’s for greater wealth, liberty or cultural freedoms that are elusive in China.
On a recent weekend in a downtown event space in Quincy, seniors in classical Chinese attire acted out the myth of the immortal moon goddess.
The Mid-Autumn Festival celebration was organized by Frank Poon of the nonprofit Civic Education Alliance. Poon came to the U.S. during a wave of Chinese immigration in the 1980s. Ronald Reagan was president, Beijing relaxed restrictions on its citizens’ ability to leave the country and the British would agree to transfer Hong Kong to Chinese control.
Poon said he knows success in the U.S. is far from guaranteed — and it often takes a lifetime of struggle.
“We’re still aiming at the American dream,” Poon said, and that people like him are “willing to invest all our time, all our effort, to make it come true.”
Looking back, Poon said he’s achieved what brought him to America 43 years ago. For him, that success has been more spiritual than something that can be measured.
“My American dream is, ‘I want to have a better life,’ ” he said. “I do have a better family. I do have opportunity to work with the community, and deep inside, in my heart and soul, I feel good.”
But one attendee of the harvest festival had something to say about a dream deferred.
In 1988, Carol Chu followed her future husband to Boston, with little money and no family here.
“The United States is such a freedom country,” she said. “I wanted to enjoy all the opportunity — get the chance to be free, live free, speak freely.”
Soon after they settled, however, Chu began to realize those things might be out of reach. She became pregnant, and her husband developed a severe gambling addiction. The worst part was when Chu lost custody of her son.
“I [was] so disappointed when I came here, because my American dream totally has not come true,” she said.
Instead of returning to her country, Chu stayed in the U.S. in order to be with her son, even if she could only see him one hour at a time.
"The United States is such a freedom country. I wanted to enjoy all the opportunity — get the chance to be free, live free, speak freely."
Chu recently retired after 37 years working for the Postal Service, and as the years have brought her closer to her son, she said she is finally happy here. Now that her boy is grown, Chu plans to split her time between China and the U.S.
“I think my duty is done,” she said.
Over the decades since these folks emigrated to the U.S., China has roared forward as an economic titan, with hundreds of millions emerging from extreme poverty. For the Chinese youth of today, that adds a new dimension to the decision to leave, whether for the U.S. or anywhere else in the world.
At Quincy’s Wollaston Beach, dozens of Chinese youth spread out on the sand, playing mahjong and practicing the Cantonese language. It was a meetup of the Boston Cantonese Club, and DJ Amanda Lou was spinning pop music under a tent.
The recent Boston University graduate is from Macau, a special administrative region of China ruled by the Portuguese until 1999. She spoke about the American ideal more in terms of culture than economic opportunities or political freedom. For her and many other Chinese graduates, Lou said, the exposure to freedom and different lifestyles is a strong motivation to stay.
“In Boston, I can just wear whatever I want, right? I can wear a tank top, shorts, walk outside — nothing will change," she said. "No one's going to stare at you."
At 23, Lou is ready to make a life in Boston. But remaining in the U.S. has never been a certainty for international students. It depends on factors like finding an employer to sponsor a visa petition. And with the current administration looking to add massive fees for foreign worker visas — and to favor “higher-skilled and higher-paid” applicants — big challenges loom for people like Lou.
“What happens if I don't find an employer who's willing to sponsor me?” she said. “Even if they do, what happens if I get fired or something? Definitely very stressful.”
Lou hopes to open a jazz bar in Boston one day, but if America is out of reach, she’ll have to bring her dreams elsewhere.
This kind of uncertainty is well-known to Vincent Lau, an immigration attorney in Boston. Much of his work involves helping American companies secure work visas. Lau said the traditional legal routes still exist, but they have increasingly narrowed under President Trump.
Among an array of measures to tighten rules on student immigration, Lau said consular officers now hold greater discretion to deny visa petitions, making it more difficult to advise parents on the wisdom of sending their kids to the U.S.
“Applying for the visas at the consulates has become much more challenging for Chinese citizens in general,” Lau said, “especially for students.”
On top of that, the administration is cutting research funding and suing elite universities, which Lau said have long been reliable paths to success in America. The administration has threatened to revoke visas for some Chinese students, and it accused Harvard of collaborating with the Chinese Communist Party.
Lau said the draw to study and live in the U.S. remains strong, but those policies are taking a toll.
“When [universities] are not being backed by the government, when they are being attacked by the government, it's not a quote-unquote, safe place,” Lau said. “It's not a place where people want to go.”
The impetus to immigrate has also changed as Chinese universities rise in global rankings. More Chinese youth are pursuing their studies in China. At the same time, an increasing number of students are returning home after graduating overseas.
But for Boston Cantonese Club organizer Alex Ng, China is no promised land. Ng said the Chinese tech economy suffers from a "race to the bottom" mentality, more driven by the search for rock bottom prices than by innovation. Ng said competition for jobs is fiercer in China than in the U.S., and that's especially hard for college grads.

‘Annihilate’ vs ‘crushing’ attacks: Why Iran, US up rhetoric amid talks
Trump threatens to ‘annihilate’ Iran and then boasts about diplomacy, provoking Tehran to warn of a ‘crushing’ response.
Speaking on the first day of the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) on Tuesday, United States President Donald Trump threatened to “annihilate” Iran. Hours later, he told reporters that US officials held a “very good” meeting with Iranian leaders.
Iran’s military did not hold back. Dismissing Trump’s remarks, the Armed Forces General Staff – Iran’s highest military body – warned that it is ready to respond with “crushing” severer attacks than earlier in the war.
- list 1 of 3Trump: US-Iran meeting at UN was ‘very good’
- list 2 of 3US Republican calls for probe into Donald Trump Jr’s business dealings
- list 3 of 3Iran cancels Baghdad, Muscat flights as US aviation sanctions take effect
Iranian Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, though not in direct response to Trump, used similarly combative imagery in a message marking the start of Iran’s academic year, describing knowledge combined with faith and morality as a “sharp sword” capable of cutting off the hands of aggressors.
Amid the rhetoric, the two sides held their first in-person meeting in months on the sidelines of the UNGA, reviving a diplomatic channel that had almost collapsed in the wake of repeated violations of the June memorandum of understanding (MoU), which subsequently lapsed last month, during nearly seven months of the US-Israel war on Iran.
The war has triggered a spike in fuel prices in the US – a major issue in the midterm elections due in November – while sanctions by Washington are squeezing Iran’s economy. While Tehran wants the economic measures as well as the US naval blockade on its ports lifted, Washington wants Iran to allow free navigation through the Strait of Hormuz, a global oil chokepoint, and an end to its nuclear programme.
So, why are Washington and Tehran engaging in diplomacy aimed at finding a way out of the war while also issuing fiery and violent threats?
What were the US-Iran talks on at the UNGA?
Trump said his envoys – Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner – met Iranian officials for about three hours on the sidelines of the UNGA. He described it as a “very good meeting”, while acknowledging the Iranian representatives were “not the highest level”.
Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi took part, with mediators shuttling between the US and Iranian teams.
Witkoff later said the discussions were completed and expressed hope they would prove “constructive and promising”.
The talks were believed to be the first in-person discussions between officials from the two countries since US Vice President JD Vance met senior Iranian officials in Switzerland in June.
Trump said another meeting was expected “in the very near future”, adding that he believed there was “a lot of momentum” towards an agreement.
Trump used his UN speech to offer Iran a choice: an opening for negotiations and simultaneously issued a threat of further destruction.
“I have a big decision to make,” Trump said. He asked whether a deal would allow Iran to “rebuild and create a far greater country”, or “do I annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly”.
“Do I drive them into hell with no chance of survival?” he added.
The Iranian delegation walked out shortly after Trump started to describe the nearly seven months of on-and-off military strikes against Iran, with only one person remaining seated.
In a statement carried by the Mehr news agency, Iran’s General Staff accused the US president of using the UN platform to justify “aggression”.
“Such words demonstrate America’s strategic dead end in its aggression against the Iranian nation,” it said, describing Trump’s repeated threats as “not a sign of power but a sign of their strategic desperation”.
The statement also warned Iran’s armed forces are ready to deliver strikes against the US and Israel that would be “more crushing and less predictable” than earlier in their war.
Khamenei also used combative language, although his remarks were not a direct response to Trump’s UN address.
In a message marking the start of the academic year, he described knowledge, faith and morality as weapons against the US and Israel.
“Power rooted in knowledge and coupled with piety and morality serves as an iron shield and a sharp sword that can cut off their aggressors’ hands from humanity,” Khamenei said, referring to what he called the “criminal US government” and Israel, Press TV reported.
Meanwhile, before departing Tehran on Tuesday, President Masoud Pezeshkian also struck a defiant tone, accusing the US of doing “everything they can to block every possible route” to force Iran and its people to surrender after failing to achieve that militarily.
Pezeshkian said Iran would use the UN gathering to highlight “the crimes that have been committed against” Iranians and the distrust created by the war.
Why the escalating rhetoric amid diplomacy?
The hostile rhetoric between Washington and Tehran should not necessarily be seen as contradicting ongoing diplomatic efforts, according to Andreas Krieg, associate professor at King’s College London.
Instead, Krieg argues, the public threats and tough language are part of a wider battle to shape how any eventual agreement is perceived at home and abroad.
“The violent rhetoric is not a contradiction to the diplomacy. It is part of the bargaining strategy,” Krieg told Al Jazeera.
For Trump, the objective is to demonstrate that Iran returned to negotiations because of the US pressure rather than any softening of Washington’s position.
Meanwhile, Iran’s leadership needs to construct almost the opposite narrative – that Tehran resisted US pressure, retained sufficient leverage and ultimately forced Washington to negotiate.
“This has become a major war over narratives as much as a war over material power,” Krieg said.
Both governments are therefore addressing several audiences simultaneously, including their domestic constituencies, each other, regional allies and the wider international community.
Moreover, Krieg said the rhetoric could, paradoxically, make an eventual compromise easier. “If both sides can convince their audiences that they negotiated from strength, they gain more political space to compromise privately without appearing to capitulate publicly,” he noted.
According to the academic, the real issue was “sequencing”.
“Iran wants movement on the blockade, sanctions and frozen assets before giving up leverage over Hormuz or accepting irreversible nuclear concessions. Washington wants tangible Iranian movement first, particularly on navigation and the nuclear file,” he said.
“Qatar’s role is crucial because Doha can turn those incompatible demands into reciprocal steps rather than forcing one side to move first. The danger is that rhetoric can still create its own momentum if there is a major attack, significant US casualties, an Israeli strike or escalation from Yemen.”

New single, new era? Following 2025’s 'The Life of a Showgirl' and her 'Toy Story 5' single, Taylor Swift has announced a new song – and the cover art is proving divisive.
She just can’t take a break...
Following her headline-dominating wedding this year, Taylor Swift has announced she’s back with a new single, titled ‘Patient Zero’, which will drop on Friday.
“I’ve been impatiently waiting to tell you that my brand new single “Patient Zero” will be out on September 25 (!!!!!!!!!!!!) and it’s available to pre-order now on my website for 24 hours,” Swift wrote on Instagram.
Her Instagram bio now reads: “And, baby, that’s sh0w business f0r y0u,” which ties back to her 'The Life of a Showgirl' era.
It isn’t confirmed whether the new track is part of a companion piece to her 2025 album or part of a new era, but many are speculating that the song’s title seems to be a reference to Swift being described as “patient zero for emotional contagion” in a 2024 LA Times article.
As is Swift’s controversial way, the release of the single on streaming will be joined by three separate CDs with different covers for the track’s standard, acoustic, and piano versions.
Quite why those three versions couldn’t be generously compiled onto one single release for avid fans who will have to shell out for three different versions remains baffling... but, baby, that’s tires0me capitalism aimed at miking fans f0r m0re m0ney f0r y0u.
One main sticking point for some fans is the cover art for ‘Patient Zero’...
Shortly after Swift’s post went viral online, it was hit with criticism from social media users who called out what they deemed to be “excessive photo editing” and a Photoshop fail.
“The Photoshop on Taylor Swift's "Patient Zero" cover is horrendous... girl, you're a billionaire, please get a professional photographer,” one person wrote on X, while another posted: “I'm so sorry but why does the side of her look so poorly edited? It looks way over-airbrushed and almost AI”.
“No shade, but they edited her armpit to HELL,” another scoffed.
Check out some reactions below:
Swift’s last album, ‘The Life of a Showgirl', came out in October 2025. In Euronews Culture’s review, we wrote that the album “doesn’t live up to the frequently exhausting fanfare” and that while “her work ethic isn't inspiring - and doesn’t seem to be entirely human (...) with playful but uninspired lyrics like “Please God, bring me a best friend who I think is hot”, a sabbatical is needed.”
Read the full review here.
In June, Swift returned to her country roots with the release of 'I Knew It, I Knew You', a track that appeared on the soundtrack of Toy Story 5.
On Sunday, the 14-time Grammy winner will receive the Inaugural MTV VMA Artist Director Honors, which will make her the most awarded artist in the award show’s history.

Ahead of US, China meeting, Trump and Xi both face crossroads | Opinion
The Chinese leader has to deal with a legitimacy crisis at home. The U.S. leader knows that Republicans' success in the midterm elections depend on economic relief for the American people, fast.
A leadership summit between any two countries is always cause for pressure-packed preparations by all relevant agencies, but for the Sept. 24 White House U.S.-China summit between President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping, the stakes have arguably never been higher.
China faces the loss of 18 million factory jobs, rampant income inequality and a 70% increase in rural protests between 2024 and 2025.
The United States faces skyrocketing oil prices, persistent threats of escalation from Iran and China’s alarming trade surplus.
For big "bilaterals" like this one set for Thursday, every Cabinet agency and all senior White House staff scurry to put together an agenda. Here are strategies they'll likely submit to the president as bases for memorandums of understanding, which will come from the meetings if executed well.
Trump, Xi should call for a world conference on AI
Trump and Xi, first and foremost, could agree to participate in and lead a world conference on artificial intelligence, with positive usages and safeguards.
Trump must seek a halt to China’s rampant intellectual property theft, which has enabled Chinese companies to save billions of dollars training their AI on American frontier models.
However, because both countries deeply mistrust the other to fairly navigate AI safety on their own, the leaders must address patent and copyright theft laws, and implement AI guardrails against human harm. Offered in a spirit of friendly competitors, this could benefit both countries and the world.
A joint statement could be significant.
Gain more rare earth metals for the United States
In 2025, Beijing began requiring foreign companies to obtain a special government-approved license to ship certain products containing rare earth metals sourced from China.
To obtain these licenses, companies had to share highly sensitive data, including profiles of end-users.
Companies affiliated with foreign militaries would be largely denied licenses unless Washington maintains some information access (now recognizing U.S. military’s dependence on Chinese rare earth elements) but the United States and China could agree on mutual assistance.
There could be higher tariffs or tighter restrictions on China’s access to semiconductors unless China withdraws its expanded license requirements.
Clarify US-China research collaboration
Recently, millions of dollars of Washington funding for colleges has helped Beijing develop critical military technology through academic research involving organizations affiliated with China’s defense industrial base, according to a House Republican report.
In response, clarify and regulate more strongly research collaboration between American universities and Chinese-military-affiliated organizations.
Negotiate guardrails on tech components that can spy
Mounting evidence reveals that Chinese tech components can secretly transmit information to China.
This is a massive national security risk, particularly due to the U.S. military’s reliance on Chinese batteries. Trump must secure restrictions on components sold to the United States with surveillance capabilities.
Maintain strategic ambiguity on Taiwan
Taiwan remains the strictest red line for China, so any diplomatic negotiation requires strategic ambiguity on Taiwan contingencies. Remain vague about whether the United States would militarily support Taiwan in the case of a Chinese invasion.
Keep the $14 billion pending Taiwan arms sale up for negotiation and leave for later after this summit, depending on Xi’s openness to other demands, and signal support for China while keeping future options open to support Taiwan if necessary.
Pledge to reduce oil prices
Washington wants Beijing to buy American goods. Unfortunately, rising oil prices from the Iran war exacerbated production costs in China, slowing down its economic growth, and driving the Chinese to buy fewer American goods.
Trump could pledge de-escalation attempts with Iran to reopen the Strait of Hormuz to bring down oil prices. Clarify that China should stop buying Iranian oil until the Strait of Hormuz is opened, and that China should expand its agreement to import more American agricultural goods.
Cooperate on drug policy, target methamphetamine and fentanyl
Expand the McCaffrey-China anti-drug agreement made more than a quarter-century ago on methamphetamine and now fentanyl.
In 2000, retired Army Gen. Barry McCaffrey, as head of the Office of National Drug Control Policy, led a delegation to China and negotiated a drug treatment and source prevention agreement. He explained that for China itself, treatment was more than warehousing thousands of addicts cold turkey in a big room in a Chinese city. It meant stop allowing import of drugs from Myanmar, formerly known as Burma, and providing jobs and counseling for addicts.
Now, China is a major source of devastating fentanyl in the United States. An agreement to help each other could be a productive component of the Trump-Xi summit.
To solidify long-term trust, Trump should increase cultural ties between the two nations by renewing a commitment to sharing arts and sports – like Chinese table tennis and U.S. football diplomacy – and inviting China’s National Peking Opera back to the United States.
Both Trump and Xi are at a crossroads
Xi faces a legitimacy crisis. While many of his citizens have long supported the Chinese Communist Party’s overall economic prosperity, China’s stagnating economy and skyrocketing youth unemployment have greatly weakened the party's internal political legitimacy.
For his part, Trump’s reversing his low approval ratings ahead of the November midterm elections (and, consequently, the Republican Party’s success) depends on his ability to deliver economic relief, and fast. That can be accomplished by increasing American exports to China.
Chinese leaders are as interested in making productive deals with the United States as we are with them, making the Trump-Xi summit an enormous opportunity for the two global superpowers as well as the world.
Robert Weiner was a spokesman in the Clinton and George W. Bush administrations, the White House drug policy spokesman, chief of staff for the House Aging Committee, and communications director of the House Government Operations and Oversight Committee. Emmbrooke Flather is a senior policy analyst at Robert Weiner Associates, and served as copresident of the Chinese Culture Club at Phillips Academy Andover. At Boston College, she studied Mandarin, East Asian Security and the Rise of China.
